Their married life had found its own rhythm, though not always easy. Reza still lived his routine as a DJ — gigs on weekends, production sessions at the studio on weekdays. Nisa, on the other hand, had resigned from her old administrative job, trying several things — calligraphy classes, volunteering at an orphanage — but not one felt like home.

That night, Nisa sat cross-legged on the studio floor, an old cardboard box open before her. She'd just taken it out of the small storage room at her parents' house, where her teenage belongings were still kept since she moved after marrying. Inside that box: old flash drives containing hundreds of EDM songs, several DJ Mag magazines whose pages had yellowed, and at the box's bottom, wrapped in flannel cloth beginning to fray — her Numark Party Mix 2, the small controller that had accompanied her practicing secretly since high school.
Reza, who had just finished Isha prayer, sat beside her, taking that small controller carefully, turning it over like someone holding a historical artifact.
“There it is,” he murmured, a smile growing on his face. “This is what you used to practice alone before?”

“For years,” Nisa answered, taking it back and placing it in her lap. “From high school until before we married. This is what made me able to hear your kick drum that time at the studio, remember? When you were surprised I could immediately match the tempo.”
“I still remember it well,” Reza laughed a little. “I kept asking you over and over, 'is this really the first time?' And you kept lying saying yes.”
“I was scared, Za,” Nisa smiled, remembering those times again. “I was scared that if I admitted it, you'd think I was weird — a Muslimah who secretly collected DJ equipment in her room.”
“I actually liked you more because of that,” Reza gripped her hand. “It took several times of us 'practicing' together at the studio before you finally came clean.”

Nisa nodded, remembering those afternoons — visit after visit to Reza's studio before they married, the excuses they made up to their respective families, the hours they spent trying simple transitions between conversations about Islam, about music, about themselves. Back then everything still felt like a small game, something fun but never truly serious — just a way to get closer to each other, not something they built earnestly.
“But that was before,” Nisa said slowly, her eyes wandering toward the small controller in her lap. “Just for fun. We never truly intended to make this something more.”
Reza looked at her, catching something in his wife's tone of voice different from usual. “Something on your mind?”

Nisa was silent briefly, choosing her words carefully. “Za, now I don't need to hide anymore. No locked drawer, no earphones I have to slip in secretly. I'm your wife. I'm free to be my whole self.” She looked at her husband directly. “I want to seriously learn this, Za. Not just occasionally like before. I want to be truly good at it. I want this to be part of my life, not just a fun little secret.”
Reza's eyes gleamed hearing it. “Are you serious, Nis?”

“Serious,” she answered firmly. “I already have the basics, right? I can already beatmatch, I already have ears you think are good. But I want more than that. I want to learn proper harmonic mixing, learn to read crowd energy, learn everything you know. I want to be a real partner, Za. Not just a spectator occasionally invited to try.”

Reza rose from his seat, pulling Nisa to stand too, bringing her to the work chair in front of the main mixer table — not the small controller in their laps, but the complete professional equipment that had all this time been his exclusive territory.
“If that's the case,” he said, seating Nisa in that chair, “starting tonight, we're no longer just playing around. I'll teach you everything. From the beginning, seriously.”
“I already know the basics, Za,” Nisa reminded him, slightly offended by that “from the beginning” tone.

“I know,” Reza smiled, pulling a second chair for himself. “I don't mean from zero. I mean, we build from what you already have, but now truly systematically. Not just trying things when relaxed. If you want to be a real partner, that needs discipline, Nis. Regular practice, not just when in the mood.”
Nisa nodded, feeling a beat different from the awkward beat when she first touched Reza's mixer years ago — this time a beat born from commitment, from a decision she'd considered thoroughly.

That night, Reza started by evaluating Nisa's existing basic ability — and he was surprised to find her foundation far stronger than he remembered from their sessions during their dating days. Nisa's ears were still as sharp as before, maybe even more, the result of years of listening critically though without much direct hand practice.

“Okay,” said Reza, after asking her to do some basic transitions which Nisa did smoothly. “Your basics are already really good, it turns out. Now let's raise the level. Harmonic mixing — do you know about the Circle of Fifths?”
“I once read about it briefly in one of my DJ Mag magazines,” Nisa answered. “But never truly practiced it.”

“Well, this is what we'll start with,” Reza opened software on the screen, showing a circular diagram with musical notes arranged around it. “This will help you choose songs that connect musically, not just by tempo.”

That night turned into a far more structured learning session than before. Reza taught more complex concepts — how to read a song's key and match it with the next song so the transition feels smooth not only rhythmically but also harmonically; how to use effects like reverb and delay to create dramatic moments in a set; how to read the audience's energy even before they themselves realize it, and adjust song choices based on that.
Nisa absorbed it all at a speed that made Reza increasingly certain his decision that night wasn't just a momentary emotional impulse, but a calling that had long been settling within his wife.

Toward midnight, after hours of practice, they paused briefly, exhausted but satisfied. Nisa leaned back in her chair, gazing at the screen still displaying the sound waves from the last track they'd worked on together.
“Za,” she said, “I want to ask something.”
“What?”
“Why before, when we were still dating, did we never think about making this serious? Even though you already knew my ability.”

Reza was silent briefly, considering his answer. “Because at that time, Nis, we had many other things that had to be settled first. Our relationship, your family, my religion. All of that was far more important than thinking about a music career together. And also—” he smiled, “—I thought you also weren't mentally ready for it. You were still too afraid of being found out, still had too much you needed to settle with yourself.”
Nisa nodded, realizing the truth in her husband's words. “Now it's different.”
“Now it's different,” Reza repeated, gripping her hand. “Now you don't have anything left that needs hiding. And that makes all the difference, Nis.”

The following weeks ran with a new rhythm far more intensive than their relaxed sessions before. Every Tuesday and Thursday night, after Maghrib, they sat in the studio, this time with a clear and structured purpose. Reza arranged a kind of unofficial curriculum — the first week focused on mastering harmonic mixing, the second week exploring effects and creative transitions, the third week simulating reading crowd energy through video recordings of his old gigs, the fourth week starting to arrange Nisa's first complete set from beginning to end.

What surprised Reza most was no longer Nisa's learning speed — he'd already guessed that would be fast, given the foundation already there. What surprised him was his wife's dedication. Nisa began bringing a special notebook for their sessions, noting every new technique, every mistake she made and how to fix it. She even began practicing alone during the day, using her old Numark as a complement to their night sessions with professional equipment.

“You,” Reza said one night, shaking his head while laughing after Nisa accurately pointed out a technical problem in one of the tracks he'd been working on for days, “it's like I'm training an athlete who already had natural talent, then went crazy with practice once she decided to get serious.”
“I am serious, Za,” Nisa answered, smiling proudly but still focused on the screen in front of her. “I don't want to be half-hearted anymore. Not now.”

One afternoon, when Reza was at the studio with Tegar for a client production session, Nisa sat alone in their apartment's living room, her small Numark connected to a laptop, headphones fitted on her head. She was practicing a complicated transition — a shift from progressive house to melodic techno needing perfect timing to feel smooth.

Between her practice, her mind occasionally wandered to the past — to her small room years ago, to the locked drawer, to the earphones she always hid every time there were footsteps approaching. Before, she often wished she had someone to share that secret with, someone who could understand without judging. But at that time, she never truly found that figure — even among her own religious study friends, not one could she truly trust to open up that side.

Strangely, now, sitting alone in her quiet apartment living room, she realized something she'd never imagined before: she no longer needed such a figure. This music, this small controller, beat after beat she arranged with her own hands — all of it was already enough to fill the space that once felt empty. Plus Reza, who understood every corner of her without her needing to explain twice. She felt full, whole, without any lack.

Alhamdulillah, she thought, smiling to herself while returning focus to the screen in front of her. She remembered how far the journey she'd traveled — from a teenage girl crying in fear alone imagining the reactions of people around her if they knew, to a grown woman now sitting in her own apartment's living room, practicing freely, fully supported by a husband who loved her as she was — and most importantly, sustained by herself, by a satisfaction no longer dependent on anyone's recognition.

She put her headphones back on, and continued practicing with new spirit — no longer just chasing technical perfection, but also honoring the long journey that had brought her to this point, alone, in her own way.

At the end of the first month of their intensive sessions, as they sat exhausted but satisfied after completing Nisa's first truly complete set — a forty-five-minute set blending the harmonic mixing she'd mastered with a personal touch reflecting her own taste — Reza looked at his wife with a serious expression he rarely showed.
“Nis,” he said, “I have an idea. But you can absolutely refuse.”
“What?”

“There's a small charity event next month, in Kemang. I've been asked to be a guest star. Small only, audience at most a hundred people, to raise funds for a street children's education foundation.” Reza took a breath. “I want you to do a set with me. Public, Nis. No longer just in this studio.”

Nisa's smile faded briefly, replaced by an expression hard to read — no longer fear from feeling incapable, but something more complicated: awareness that this would be a step that couldn't be taken back, the moment when the world she'd guarded so tightly all this time would open for the first time before people she didn't know.
“I'm ready technically, Za,” she said slowly. “But public… that's a different story.”

“I know,” Reza gripped her hand tightly. “But I really believe, you're ready. Not just because of your ability. But because I've seen myself how you've changed this month — from hesitant, to confident in yourself.”

Nisa looked at her husband for a long time, considering every word just spoken. Within her, fear of public judgment and the courage she'd built over the last weeks wrestled fiercely — a new battle different from her battle in her teenage years, but just as heavy.
But this time, she wasn't alone in that battle.
“Okay,” she finally said, her voice soft but firm. “I'm in.”

Reza smiled widely, pulling his wife into a tight embrace, kissing her forehead, then her cheek, then — with a gentleness that seemed to want to convey all his pride and love at once — her lips. That night, after the studio lights were turned off and the controllers returned to rest in their place, the warmth they shared continued far beyond conversation about stages and music, becoming another language just as important in their marriage — a language they never told anyone about, but always became the anchor uniting every big decision they took together.

Outside their apartment window, Jakarta's sky that had been blanketed by rain began showing stars between clouds starting to thin. But inside, something long buried now truly rose — no longer just a fun secret hobby, but a commitment that, though not one of them fully realized it that night, would become the first step of a journey far bigger than they ever imagined.
2: An outdoor cafe in Kemang, South Jakarta — One month later

That promised day finally arrived in a way that felt too fast for Nisa. Throughout the previous month, their practice sessions in the apartment's small studio grew increasingly intensive — no longer about mastering basic techniques she already had, but sharpening precision, building performance stamina, and the most challenging: practicing performing as if there were an audience, though only Reza witnessed.
“Again,” Reza said that night, three days before the event, after Nisa completed her third run-through that night. “The transition at the fifth minute still feels hesitant.”
“I'm already tired, Za,” Nisa rested her head on the sofa, her eyes closed. “It's already eleven at night.”

“I know. But this is no longer about whether you understand the technique or not, Nis. You're already skilled. This is about your confidence in front of people. Every time you hesitate, that's audible, even though your hands are already automatically correct.”
Nisa opened her eyes, looking at her husband sitting in the chair beside her. “I'm scared, Za. Not scared of pressing the wrong button. I'm scared of… how people will see me.”

“I know that's the hardest part,” Reza answered gently. “But you don't need to prove your ability anymore, Nis. I've seen for myself, you're already more than ready technically. What remains is only the courage to show it to the world.”

That night they practiced until almost dawn, no longer repeating technique, but simulating stage pressure — Reza occasionally deliberately made noise, pretending to be a rowdy audience, even occasionally turning off one of the audio channels suddenly to see how Nisa reacted under pressure.
“If that actually happens later,” he explained, “you have to stay calm. Panic is what makes a small mistake into a big mistake.”

Between her practice, Nisa also began thinking about practical things she'd never considered before — how to make sure her gamis and hijab stayed neat and comfortable while moving actively behind the deck, how to arrange prayer time between the soundcheck schedule and performance, how to answer if someone asked directly about her identity as a Muslimah who became a DJ.
“I've prepared a standard answer,” she said one night to Reza, half joking half serious. “If someone asks why I DJ but wear hijab, I'll say: why not?”
Reza laughed hearing it. “Simple, but right on target.”
“I've also thought about the prayer schedule,” Nisa continued more seriously. “I want to still be able to pray on time, even in the middle of an event. That's important to me, Za. Non-negotiable.”
“I've already spoken to the committee,” Reza nodded. “They've prepared a small room behind the stage for us both if we need to pray before or after the set.”

That readiness, however small it sounded, gave Nisa additional calm ahead of that big day — proof that Reza truly paid attention to every aspect of her, not just her technical ability behind the deck.

D-Day arrived with a clear cloudless Jakarta sky. That charity event was held at a small outdoor cafe, its theme simple — fundraising for the Cahaya Kecil Foundation. Its stage was no more than a half-meter-high wooden platform, decorated with string lights, with a sound system that though not as luxurious as the big clubs where Reza usually performed, was adequate enough for the estimated hundred-some crowd attending.

Nisa stood behind the stage, wearing a long olive-green gamis she'd chosen herself days before, paired with a matching hijab she'd arranged in a style that felt right for her — elegant but not rigid, sharia-compliant but still having a personal touch reflecting who she was. Her hands were cold and slightly trembling, her heart pounding hard — not because of doubt in her ability, but because of awareness that in a few minutes, the secret she'd guarded so tightly since her teens would be displayed before people who didn't know her at all.
“Are you okay?” Reza asked, appearing beside her, already wearing a simple black t-shirt with headphones circling his neck as usual.

“I'm so nervous, Za,” she admitted honestly, her voice nearly a whisper. “Not about whether I can or can't. I know I can. But… what if people see me as weird? A hijab-wearing Muslimah who suddenly became a DJ?”

Reza gripped both her hands, looking straight into her eyes. “Nis, listen to me. You've practiced for months. You have an ability that even professional DJs need years to reach. What remains is only one thing: daring to show who you are to the world.”
“Bismillah,” Nisa whispered, taking a long breath, trying to calm her heartbeat still racing hard.
“Bismillah,” Reza repeated, kissing her forehead briefly before guiding her up onto that small stage.
Several days earlier, when Reza first told his manager, Jason, that Nisa would perform at the Kemang event, the bespectacled man's reaction was far from enthusiastic.

“Are you sure, Rez?” Jason asked at the time, looking at Reza via video call, his brows furrowed. “I know you love Nisa, but this isn't just about being romantic. This is public. Once people see, it can't be taken back.”

“I know the risk, Jas,” Reza answered calmly. “But this isn't a gimmick, and this also isn't Nisa who just learned yesterday afternoon. She's practiced for years alone, and this last month we've practiced together seriously every day. She truly has ability, Jas.”

“Okay, I believe about her ability,” Jason nodded, though his tone of voice was still hesitant. “What I'm worried about is people's reaction. You know yourself how our netizens are. A hijab-wearing DJ is… that will become talking material, whether positive or negative.”
Reza was silent briefly, considering his manager's words. “I've already talked about this with Nisa. She decided herself, with open eyes. I just want to support whatever she chooses.”
Jason let out a long sigh at the other end of the phone, then smiled a little. “Okay. I trust you, Rez. But if anything happens, I'm here to help, okay?”

The cheers of that small crowd welcomed them as soon as they went up on stage — warm applause, some whistles, curious faces looking at the hijab-wearing woman figure standing beside DJ Rez G who was already quite well known among Jakarta's electronic music lovers.

Reza started the set with the opening track they'd planned together. Nisa stood beside him, waiting her turn, her heart still pounding but her hands already ready — the result of dozens of hours of practice that had formed instinct no longer requiring conscious thought to work.

When the time came for her first transition, Nisa stepped forward, her hand approaching the deck Reza had prepared for her. For a split second, the awareness of hundreds of pairs of eyes looking at her made her heart nearly stop.

But then her hands moved on their own, following the instinct she'd trained for years — since the small Numark in her room, since the secret sessions at Reza's studio while still dating, since the last month of ceaseless practice. Her transition was smooth, on time, full of the personal touch distinguishing her from any DJ.
She glanced toward Reza, and saw a proud smile on his face — a smile that made all her fears slowly melt, replaced by pure joy.
Among the crowd, a young hijab-wearing woman standing in the front row looked at Nisa with gleaming eyes. After the event finished, she managed to push through to near the stage.

“Sis,” she said, her voice trembling between nervous and excited, “I never expected to see a DJ wearing hijab like you. I also really love music like this, but I always thought it didn't fit my identity as a Muslimah.”

Nisa looked at that young girl, recognizing herself years ago in the glint of her eyes. “There's nothing wrong with that, dear. What matters is our intention, and how we guard ourselves within it. This music is just a medium. Our identity stays whole.”
That girl's eyes teared up. “Thank you, Sis. This means so much to me.”

At the end of the set, when their last song faded slowly, festive applause filled that small cafe. Nisa stood there, breath panting, thin sweat wetting her forehead behind her hijab, but the smile radiating on her face was the most sincere smile Reza had ever seen since they married.
“You did it,” Reza whispered, embracing her briefly.
“We did it,” Nisa corrected, her eyes teary but full of happiness. “Za, I… I finally truly feel like my whole self. In front of many people, not just in our studio, just the two of us.”

Someone in the crowd recorded a short video of their performance, uploading it that very night with the caption: “DJ Rez G turns out to have a secret partner — his own wife, and she's really good. Who would've thought.”
On the drive home, Nisa rested her head against the car window, gazing at the city lights twinkling past the glass wet with thin drizzle. “Za, this is just the beginning, right?”
“This is just the beginning,” Reza repeated, gripping her hand tightly throughout the drive home. “I can feel it, Nis. This is only the first step of something far bigger.”

The next morning, that video had been watched several thousand times, with comments split between sincere praise and cynicism Nisa had long guessed would appear. But this time, reading those comments, she no longer felt intimidated as she might have a year ago.
“I've decided,” she said to Reza while sipping her morning coffee, “I don't want to live for other people's validation anymore. I want to live for what I believe is right.”
Reza smiled proudly, reaching for his wife's hand on the table. “That's my wife.”
That afternoon, Nisa's phone rang. The name displayed on the screen made her heart pound — Mother.
With slightly trembling hands, she answered that call. “Assalamualaikum, Ma.”
“Waalaikumsalam, Nis.” Fatima's voice sounded calm, her tone hard to guess. “Mother… Mother saw the video. Aunt Wati sent it to the family group.”
Nisa closed her eyes briefly, preparing herself for the worst possibility. “Ma, I can explain—”
“Nisa,” Fatima cut in gently. “Mother isn't calling to be angry.”

A brief silence, before Fatima continued, her voice beginning to tremble with emotion hard to recognize. “Mother saw you in that video, Nis. You looked… happy. Truly happy, not forced happiness. Mother remembers before, when you were a teenager, you were often gloomy without Mother understanding why. Now Mother understands.”
Tears began pooling at the corner of Nisa's eyes. “Ma…”

“Mother isn't saying Mother immediately agrees with everything, Nis,” Fatima continued honestly. “This is still a new thing for Mother. But Mother saw Reza beside you in that video, guarding you, proud of you. And Mother saw her child finally become herself completely. That… that's what's most important for Mother.”
“Thank you, Ma,” Nisa whispered, tears now flowing freely on her cheeks. “This means so much.”
“Your father still needs time,” Fatima added carefully. “You know your father, Nis. But let Mother talk to him slowly.”
After that call ended, Nisa sat silent briefly, letting her emotions settle. Reza who had been sitting beside her, waiting patiently, finally asked, “Everything okay?”
“Everything is more than okay, Za,” Nisa answered, smiling widely amid tears still wetting her face. “My mother… my mother is proud.”

That night, Nisa opened her performance video again, reading one by one the comments that kept increasing — most full of support, some from strangers who admitted being inspired. One comment from an audience member who attended that night made her smile: “Sis, I cried seeing you perform. So brave to be yourself.”

Nisa looked at that screen for a long time, feeling the warmth spreading though that comment came from someone she'd never even known. There was its own satisfaction, she realized, in finding validation not from a narrow close circle, but from a far wider world — from people who saw her as she was, without long history, without old prejudice.

Closing her phone, Nisa rested her head on Reza's shoulder as he sat beside her on their living room sofa. Outside the window, Jakarta that night was still busy as usual, unaware of the small but deep change that had just occurred in the life of one of its residents — a woman who, after years living in two separate worlds, had finally found a way to unite them, one beat at a time, before the people she loved.
“Za,” Nisa whispered in that silence, “do you remember, when we were still dating, I once said I was afraid the two different Nisas would never be able to meet?”
“I remember,” Reza answered slowly, kissing the top of her head. “The first night you tried my mixer.”

“They've met now, Za,” Nisa said, her voice trembling with emotion. “Not just in our studio, just the two of us. But in front of Mother, in front of strangers who watched that video. The Nisa who prays five times a day, and the Nisa who's good at DJing. They've finally become one whole person.”

Reza didn't answer with words. He only embraced his wife tighter, letting that night's silence become witness to a moment that, though simple, marked the end of an inner battle that had gone on for years — and the beginning of a new chapter that, without them fully realizing it, would take them far beyond what they'd ever imagined.

That night ended in their room, Jakarta's twinkling city lights the only witness besides themselves — a celebration of gratitude unspoken through words, but fully conveyed through every touch, every closeness they shared as husband and wife who that night felt more united than before, in everything they had together.
3: Jakarta — Two months later

The video of their performance in Kemang, which initially was only watched by a few thousand people, slowly found its own life in cyberspace. Someone reposted it to an electronic music community account with a far larger follower count, and from there, its viewer numbers surged — tens of thousands, then hundreds of thousands within weeks.
Nisa first realized the scale of that change when she opened her Instagram one morning and found follow requests from people she didn't know at all — not just dozens, but hundreds overnight.
“Za,” she called, her voice slightly panicked, holding out her phone toward Reza who was brewing morning coffee. “Look at this.”
Reza took that phone, scrolled briefly, then whistled softly. “Wow. This… this is no longer 'kind of viral' level, Nis. This is really big.”
“What should I do?”
“No need to panic first,” Reza set that phone back down, gripping his wife's hand. “This isn't a bad thing. Just… needs adjustment.”

Throughout that day, both their phones vibrated ceaselessly — messages from old friends who suddenly reappeared after years without news, comments from Reza's colleagues in the music industry who were surprised to learn about his wife's other side, even unknown calls from several numbers later known to be journalists trying to contact them directly.
“This is crazy, Za,” Nisa sat on the sofa, staring at her phone screen continuously displaying new notifications. “I never expected it would be this fast.”
“Me neither,” Reza sat beside her, embracing her. “But we face this together, Nis. Like usual.”

That adjustment came faster than they expected. Within a week, a big entertainment news portal contacted Jason, requesting an exclusive interview with “DJ Rez G and his viral mysterious wife.” A few days later, another portal followed, then a radio station, then a talk show program on cable television focused on urban young people's lifestyle.
Jason arranged a strategy meeting in his small office, a room on the third floor of a building in the Kemang area full of music festival posters and award trophies lined up on shelves.

“Okay,” Jason said, opening his laptop, displaying a list of interview requests that kept increasing. “This is the situation. You have really big momentum now. The question is, what do you want to do with this momentum?”
Nisa sat restlessly in her chair. “I… I've never been interviewed about this before, Jas. I don't know what to say.”

“That's natural,” Jason nodded. “But listen, Nis — these people are curious about you not because they want to judge you. They're curious because you represent something they rarely see. A devout hijab-wearing Muslimah, who still holds her principles, but also has passion in a world they thought impossible for someone like you.”

“That's what I'm afraid of, Jas,” Nisa sighed. “What if they misunderstand? What if this is instead considered me damaging Islam's image, or considered me just seeking sensation using religious identity?”
Reza gripped his wife's hand under the table. “That's why we have to choose the right platform, and we have to control the narrative ourselves, Nis. Not let other people determine who you are.”
Jason nodded in agreement. “Rez is right. I suggest we start with just one interview, on a credible platform, one with a good track record on diversity issues. Not one just seeking clickbait.”

After long discussion, they decided to accept one interview request — from a senior journalist named Ratih known for her in-depth and balanced coverage on socio-cultural issues, including sensitive topics around Islam and modernity.

That interview took place at a quiet cafe in the Senopati area, far from the bustle of cameras and spotlights usually accompanying celebrity interviews. Ratih, a woman in her early forties with sharp but warm eyes, posed questions carefully, giving Nisa room to answer honestly without feeling cornered.
“Many people are curious,” Ratih began, “how you see your identity as a Muslimah and as a DJ. For some people, those two things seem contradictory.”

Nisa took a breath, remembering again the conversations she'd practiced with Reza many times before this interview. “For me, those two things have never truly conflicted, Kak Ratih. Music is just a medium. What determines whether it's halal or haram, good or not good, that's not the medium, but the intention and how we carry it out. I still pray five times a day, I still guard my aurat, I still hold my principles as a Muslimah. This DJing is just one way I express myself, the same as other people expressing through painting, through writing, through anything.”
“But you're not worried about public perception? About people who might consider this inappropriate?”

“I'm worried,” Nisa admitted honestly. “But I also believe, if I keep living to avoid people's judgment, I'll never become my whole self. I've tried that for years, Kak. Hiding part of myself for the sake of being accepted by others. And that didn't make me happy. This—” she moved her hand, as if pointing at the whole situation they were discussing, “—this makes me happy. And I believe, Islam is a religion that supports happiness coming from sincerity, not from pretense.”
Ratih smiled, writing something in her notes. “That's an honest answer. I like that.”

The interview continued for almost two hours, discussing various aspects — from Nisa's journey finding her love for EDM since her teens, to how she and Reza supported each other in carrying out their religious principles amid an industry full of temptation. Reza, who sat beside Nisa throughout the interview, added his own perspective occasionally, but deliberately gave larger room for his wife to speak.

“What I admire most about Nisa,” Reza said at the end of the interview, when Ratih asked how he felt seeing his wife become a public spotlight, “is that she never sacrificed who she is for the sake of being accepted by others. She's still the same Nisa — devout, gentle, full of principles — only now the world can see that too.”

That article was published a week later with a title that, though provocative, felt honest and not sensational: “The Hijab-Wearing Muslimah DJ Who Shook Indonesia's EDM World — and Why That's Not a Contradiction.”

The reaction that emerged far exceeded their expectations. That article was shared thousands of times, triggering wide discussion on social media — mostly positive, praising Nisa's courage and sincerity, but not a few also skeptical or even critical, questioning the appropriateness of a Muslimah appearing in the nightlife entertainment world.

Nisa read some of those comments with a pounding heart, but this time, with Reza beside her and the support she'd built — from her mother, from thousands of people who admired her sincerely — she felt she had a foundation sturdy enough not to be shaken by every negative comment that appeared.

However, not all criticism was that easy to ignore. One night, a sermon video from an ustaz quite well known on social media circulated widely, explicitly touching on the “hijab-wearing DJ” phenomenon as an example of the young generation's moral decline, without naming Nisa directly but clearly referring to her.
Nisa watched that video with trembling hands, tears beginning to pool. “Za, am I wrong? Have I done something wrong?”

Reza immediately sat beside her, embracing her tightly. “Nis, listen to me. One opinion, even from an ustaz, doesn't mean that's absolute truth. Other scholars have different views. You already asked our own ustaz, right? What did Ustaz Rahman say?”

Several weeks earlier, Nisa had indeed consulted with Ustaz Rahman — the Qur'an teacher who had long guided her family — to ensure that the path she chose didn't fundamentally contradict her religious principles.

“Ustaz Rahman said,” Nisa remembered that conversation again, her voice beginning to calm, “music itself is disputed among scholars, but not something absolutely forbidden, especially if not accompanied by other sins. What matters is guarding intention, guarding aurat, guarding prayer times, and guarding against elements clearly prohibited, like alcohol or free association.”

“Well, there it is,” Reza nodded. “You've checked all that, Nis. You've guarded everything carefully. One video from someone who doesn't even know you personally shouldn't shake all the effort and conviction you've built.”
Nisa let out a long sigh, resting her head on her husband's shoulder. “Thank you, Za. I just… sometimes there are still moments I feel doubt.”
“That's human,” Reza kissed her forehead. “But you're not alone facing that doubt. We're together.”

The next day, unexpectedly, support instead came from an unexpected direction — several quite influential dakwah accounts on social media actually defended Nisa, explaining with more moderate arguments that difference of scholarly opinion about music is a natural thing in Islam, and that judging someone without knowing their intention and life context is a less wise attitude.

That debate, instead of dampening the spotlight on Nisa, actually further expanded its reach — this time not only as an entertainment phenomenon, but as part of a wider discourse about how the young Muslim generation navigates their identity in the modern world.

In the following months, interview and collaboration requests kept coming. A well-known Muslim fashion brand contacted them, wanting to make Nisa their ambassador — not to promote products commercially alone, but for a campaign emphasizing that being a devout Muslimah doesn't mean having to limit oneself from personal passion and aspirations.
Nisa considered that offer carefully, discussing at length with Reza, even asking her mother's opinion.
“Ma, what do you think if I accept this offer?” she asked one afternoon, sitting in her parents' living room, a place that now felt far warmer to her compared to the last few years.

Fatima, who had now fully accepted her daughter's life path though still with some natural worries of a mother, answered wisely. “As long as your intention is good, Nis, and you don't leave your principles, Mother thinks that's good. You can become an example for many young people who might have the same struggle as you did before.”

Even Ahmed, her father, who still needed longer time to fully accept his daughter's life path, began showing signs of small change. One night, without Nisa knowing, she found her father watching one of her performance videos on his phone, volume turned down but his eyes fixed on the screen with an expression hard to read — a mix between old worry and something starting to resemble pride he was reluctant to admit openly.

Her mother's words, and the small signs from her father, strengthened Nisa's decision. And with her family's blessing slowly growing, Reza's full support, and her own increasingly sturdy conviction, she accepted that offer.

The campaign photoshoot day took place at a minimalist photo studio in the Kebayoran area, filled with a professional crew, stylists, and a talented young photographer who had long admired Nisa's journey from afar.

“We want to capture your essence as it is, Kak Nisa,” the photographer explained before the session began. “Not an excessively polished version. We want people to see, this is really you — a devout Muslimah, who also dares to chase her passion.”

That campaign's concept was simple but powerful: a series of photos showing Nisa in various moments of her life — wearing an elegant gamis while holding a Qur'an mushaf in one photo, then in the next photo standing confidently behind a DJ deck in equally elegant Muslim attire, headphones circling her neck. The message was clear: two worlds all this time considered impossible to unite, turned out could live side by side harmoniously in one whole person.

Reza was present accompanying throughout the session, occasionally giving small input, but mostly just sitting in the corner of the room with a proud smile, witnessing his wife shine before the camera with confidence far different from the nervous woman who once hesitantly touched a mixer for the first time.
“You look extraordinary, Nis,” he whispered between costume changes, kissing her cheek briefly.
“Thank you for always being there, Za,” Nisa answered, her eyes gleaming happily. “I would never have reached this point without you.”

That campaign, when it was finally launched several weeks later, reaped a reception far exceeding that brand's expectations — shared widely, praised for its courage in displaying representation rarely seen in the Muslim fashion industry or the entertainment industry in general. Nisa received hundreds of messages from Muslim women throughout Indonesia, even from neighboring countries, who felt inspired to be braver in chasing their own passion without sacrificing their beliefs.

The night after that long and exhausting photoshoot day, Nisa and Reza came home to their apartment far later than usual. Nisa still wore the remains of heavy makeup from the photo session, her body tired but her heart full — an exhaustion that felt sweet, not torturous.
“I want to shower first,” she said, taking off her shoes in front of the door.

“I'll help take off those earrings,” Reza offered, approaching from behind, his fingers moving gently to open the earring clasp on his wife's ear, a brief kiss landing on the nape of her neck before Nisa had a chance to turn around.

That night passed slowly and warmly, far from camera spotlights and that day's busyness — just the two of them, the closeness they shared as husband and wife who, amid all the big changes beginning to happen in their lives, still found their way home to each other every night.

Amid that wave of appreciation, a new step — whose scale they hadn't fully realized — had begun. Nisa was no longer just the wife of a famous DJ who happened to go viral. She began transforming into a public figure with her own voice and influence, an identity that, in the coming years, would take her far beyond music festival stages toward something even she herself hadn't yet dared to fully imagine.
4: 2028 — Two years later

Within two years, “Rez & Nis” — the stage name they chose together, simple and honest — became one of the most sought-after duos at Southeast Asian electronic music festivals. The journey from a small cafe in Kemang toward those magnificent stages didn't happen overnight, but through a series of steps they built carefully, one after another.

After the success of that Muslim fashion campaign, offers began flowing in heavily. Local festival promoters began contacting Jason, curious about this unique duo phenomenon. Reza and Nisa, with mature consideration, chose not to immediately accept all offers — they wanted to ensure every stage they stepped on aligned with the values they held.

Their big debut came at Djakarta Warehouse Project that year — not as headliners, but as performers on one of the secondary stages, but still becoming a main media spotlight because this was the first time Nisa performed before a crowd numbering thousands.
Backstage at DWP, performance night

“Are you ready?” Reza asked, looking at his wife standing in front of a small mirror in their dressing room, making sure her hijab was perfectly fitted, a long black gamis with golden embroidery details they'd specially chosen for that night.

“I'm always nervous before going up,” Nisa answered honestly, though the smile on her face showed confidence far different from the woman trembling on the small Kemang stage two years ago. “But this is a different nervous now. Not nervous afraid of failing. Nervous excited.”
Reza smiled, kissing her forehead. “That's extraordinary progress, Nis.”

Outside, tens of thousands of people had packed the festival area, and though their stage wasn't the main stage, the enthusiasm welcoming their arrival on stage that night felt just as festive. The big screen behind them displayed visuals specially designed — a blend of Islamic geometry with sound wave animation pulsing following the music, a visual representation of the philosophy they carried: two different worlds, uniting in harmony.

Their set that night lasted a full hour — far longer and more complex than the simple twenty minutes in Kemang. Nisa, who had now mastered the advanced techniques Reza taught years ago, led most of the transitions confidently, occasionally improvising with surprising song choices but always on target, making the crowd cheer every time an unexpected song entered smoothly into the running musical flow.

At a certain point in their set, Reza deliberately gave full room for Nisa to lead for ten full minutes — a moment they'd planned together as a symbol that this was no longer just a performance of “DJ Rez G and his wife,” but an equal collaboration between two musicians who complemented each other.

The cheers welcoming every one of Nisa's transitions that night felt like validation of the long journey she'd traveled — from the locked drawer in her teenage bedroom, to the biggest music festival stage in Indonesia.
Kuala Lumpur, several months later

The invitation to perform at a big electronic music festival in Kuala Lumpur became one of the most memorable moments in their journey that year — not because of the stage's scale, but because of an unexpected meeting after their performance finished.

A young Malaysian woman, wearing a pastel-colored tudung, approached them in the meet-and-greet area the committee had prepared. Her eyes teary, her hands slightly trembling as she held out a small notebook to be signed.

“Kak Nisa,” she said, her voice trembling holding back emotion, “I… I'm learning electronic music production now. Before this, my family didn't approve. They said it wasn't suitable work for a Muslim woman. But after seeing you, I worked up the courage to tell my mother. And… and she's starting to understand.”

Nisa looked at that young girl, feeling a familiar wave of emotion — recognition of herself years ago, the same fear, the same hope. She gripped that girl's hand tightly. “I'm proud of you. Keep up your effort, and never stop being yourself.”
After that girl left, Reza looked at his wife whose eyes were still teary. “Are you okay?”
“I'm more than okay, Za,” Nisa smiled, wiping her eyes. “Moments like this make me realize, this isn't just about music. This is about giving other people permission to be themselves.”

That moment, though brief, embedded deeply in Nisa's heart — one of the increasingly many similar encounters that began happening every time they performed in various cities. Young women approaching with teary eyes, telling how Nisa's courage gave them permission to chase their own dreams, though different from the expectations of the society around them.

That night's success opened new doors they'd never imagined before. Invitations began coming from festivals in Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, even Singapore. They also got to open sets for several big international names touring Southeast Asia, an experience giving them exposure on a far wider scale.

However, amid the busyness of stages and spotlights, there was one thing that never changed: their routine together. Congregational prayer in the dressing room before going on stage, without compromise even though the soundcheck schedule sometimes had to be adjusted. Nisa who always took time to read a few verses before the set began, a small ritual that became her anchor amid the glitter of a world that could easily make people forget themselves.

Their popularity also brought small changes in daily life they'd never imagined before. Shopping at the supermarket near their apartment was now often interspersed with photo requests from other visitors who recognized them. Eating at their favorite restaurant in the Senopati area sometimes had to be booked through a private room so there wouldn't be too much disturbance. Nisa, who once lived a nearly anonymous life as an ordinary administrative staff member, now had to adapt to the reality that her face was recognized by people she'd never even met before.

“Sometimes I miss being an ordinary person, Za,” she admitted once, after a simple visit to a minimarket turned into an impromptu photo session with a dozen people. “Not that I'm ungrateful. Just… sometimes it's tiring too.”

“I understand, Nis,” Reza embraced her. “But remember, every time that happens, it also means you've touched someone else's life in a meaningful way. That's a price that, though heavy, is worth its impact.”

Nights like that, when the outside world felt too crowded and demanding, they both had their own way to find each other again — locking the hotel room door in whatever city they were staying, turning off phones, and letting that noisy world wait outside while they both created a small bubble containing only the two of them, far from camera spotlights and stage demands — a simple reminder that behind all that glitter, they remained a husband and wife who needed the same warmth from each other as before, before the world knew their names.

“Sometimes I think,” Nisa said one night in the second year of their journey, looking out the car window driving on Bangkok streets wet with tropical rain, after their performance at a big festival there, “is this really what I want to do with my life?”
Reza glanced toward her, his hand still on the wheel even though they used a private driver that night, sitting in the back seat together. “What do you mean?”

“This music… I love it so much. But sometimes there's a feeling like… there's something bigger waiting for me to do. I don't know what. Just a feeling.” Nisa sighed, trying to arrange words she found hard to define clearly. “Like there's a part of me not yet fully used, Za. We've made thousands of people happy through our music. But I feel… I want to make an impact more than that.”

Reza didn't answer immediately. He only nodded slowly, storing that sentence somewhere within himself — because somehow, he felt this wasn't just a momentary complaint after the fatigue of a long tour, but something far deeper, something that had long been growing quietly within his wife.

Returning to Jakarta, Nisa sat alone one afternoon on their penthouse balcony, gazing at the city glitter stretching wide — a view that once, years ago, she could only imagine from her small bedroom window.

Sometimes I still can't believe it myself, she thought, recalling the long journey she'd traveled — from a girl crying in fear hiding earphones behind her hijab, to a woman who now performed before tens of thousands of people in various countries.
She questioned herself, honestly without needing to answer anyone: I'm happy, right?

The answer came without doubt — yes, she was happy, truly happy. But lately, there was a feeling she found hard to explain even to herself. Like there was an empty space this music, however successful, couldn't fully fill.

She thought about that alone, without needing to tell anyone, without needing validation from outside herself. Precisely in that solitude, she realized something — how far she'd stepped, not only from hiding to being open, but also from depending on others' recognition to becoming someone who found enough honesty within herself.
Several weeks later, Jakarta
Returning from their series of Southeast Asian tours, Nisa and Reza found themselves with a slightly looser schedule — a break time they rarely had amid the busyness that kept increasing.

One afternoon, when they were relaxing in their apartment now grown larger — a penthouse unit they'd moved into a year earlier along with their increasing income — Nisa sat on the balcony, gazing at the Jakarta city view stretching wide before her, a cup of warm tea in her hand, small earphones fitted, replaying a recording of one of their sets in Kuala Lumpur.

She closed her eyes, letting the bass pounding and synth layers flow, feeling again the euphoria of thousands of people moving in unison that night — strange bodies that for a few hours melted into one unity through the same rhythm. There was something scientific and spiritual at once about that, she thought — how sound frequency could align hundreds of people's heartbeats at once, how free body movement without burden could become the most honest form of release she'd ever known.

And from there, her mind wandered — as had been happening increasingly often lately — to years ago, to her old small room, to earphones that had to be hidden, to the fear every time someone walked too close. To how long she'd had to struggle alone just to feel what she now felt freely every night on stage — pure joy without guilt, a body moving without being judged, a soul uniting with others through something as beautiful as music.

Why was this so strictly forbidden before, she thought. Why was something that turned out to be as healthy and beautiful as this, which could unite so many people in sincere happiness, considered so dangerous for a young girl?
Reza joined her, sitting in the chair beside her. “You look deep in thought.”

“I'm thinking about how it felt before, Za,” Nisa admitted, taking off her earphones. “Completely forbidden from feeling all this. Even though this… this is what freed me most from anything I've ever felt.”
“Do you know what it is?” Reza asked, though not yet fully understanding where his wife's thoughts were heading.
Nisa shook her head slowly. “Not fully yet. But I'm starting to feel… there's something I have to do with this restlessness, outside the stage and the lights.”

Reza gripped her hand, looking at his wife's face gazing far toward the city horizon. Though he didn't yet fully understand where his wife's thoughts were heading, he felt something important beginning to form — the seed of a new journey that, though its shape wasn't yet clear, would soon change the direction of both their lives fundamentally.
“Whatever it is, Nis,” he said gently, “I'll be beside you to find out together.”
Nisa rested her head on her husband's shoulder, gazing at city lights beginning to twinkle one by one. “Za, can I tell you something? Something I've never told you.”
“Of course,” Reza kissed the top of her head, giving room for his wife to speak.
“There's something from my past,” Nisa began, her voice soft but firm, “that I buried a very long time ago. Something related to why I was so afraid to be honest about this music before.”
Reza waited patiently, feeling an unusual seriousness in his wife's tone of voice.

“I'm not ready to tell the details now, Za,” Nisa continued, looking at her husband with eyes full of emotion she couldn't fully define. “But I feel… it has something to do with the restlessness I've been feeling lately. Like there's a part of me I've long hidden, even longer than the earphones in my hijab before.”

Reza embraced her tighter, not forcing to know further, only giving his presence as a stable anchor amid the emotional turmoil his wife was experiencing. “Whenever you're ready to tell, Nis, I'm here. I won't force you.”

“Thank you, Za,” Nisa whispered, unexpected tears pooling at the corner of her eyes — not tears of sadness, but something more complicated, a mix between fear and hope beginning to rise after years buried.

In the distance, Jakarta's city lights began turning on one by one as dusk fell, an ocean of light stretching wide — a city that had witnessed their journey from a small studio full of dreams, to the magnificent stages that were now part of their daily life. But behind that glitter, something new began moving within Nisa — a restlessness that, though she didn't yet fully understand it, would soon lead her to the most decisive chapter in her life's journey.
5: Jakarta — Early 2029
It all started with an exhaustion that felt different.

Nisa was used to post-tour fatigue — sore muscles, hoarse voice, messed-up sleep from crossing time zones. But the exhaustion she'd felt since returning from the series of festivals in the Philippines a few weeks ago felt different: deeper, more burdening, accompanied by migraines coming without clear pattern and nausea that sometimes struck in the morning without a reason she could explain.
“Are you okay, Nis?” Reza asked one morning, finding his wife sitting pale on the edge of the bed, her hand covering her mouth holding back nausea that had suddenly struck.
“Just tired it seems, Za,” Nisa answered weakly, resting her head on her husband's shoulder as soon as her nausea subsided. “Our schedule has been insane lately.”

Reza nodded, though there was a small furrow on his forehead that didn't fully disappear. He noticed small details he'd begun to realize over the past few weeks — Nisa who usually finished her morning coffee without problem, now grimaced every time she smelled its aroma. Nisa who was usually the most enthusiastic between them when designing a new set, now more often asked to rest earlier.
The turning point came when Nisa, while counting days on her phone calendar to schedule the next practice session, suddenly fell silent, her face turning pale.
“Za,” she called, her voice trembling strangely.
Reza who was working on something on his laptop turned. “What's wrong, Nis?”
“I… I'm late,” Nisa stared at the calendar on her screen, counting again with fingers beginning to tremble. “It's been two weeks, Za. I've never been this careless about the schedule.”
Reza was silent briefly, processing his wife's words, before his eyes widened full of hope he hadn't yet dared to speak. “You think…?”
“I don't know,” Nisa bit her lip, a mix of hope and anxiety she found hard to define. “But maybe we should… check?”

That night, after Reza returned from the pharmacy with a plastic bag he tried to hide though his hands were slightly trembling, they both sat in their apartment bathroom, waiting with held breath in front of a small test pack lying on the sink.
Two red lines appeared, clear and undeniable.

Nisa covered her mouth with both hands, tears immediately pooling in her eyes. Reza, standing beside her, was silent for a few seconds that felt like forever, before finally a happy laugh he couldn't hold back burst from his lips.
“Nis,” he whispered, his voice trembling with emotion, embracing his wife tightly. “We… we're going to have a child.”
“I'm pregnant, Za,” Nisa repeated those words as if trying to convince herself this was real. “I'm really pregnant.”

They embraced for a long time in that small bathroom, tears of happiness mixed with uncontrollable laughter, a simple moment but one they would remember forever as one of the purest points in both their life journeys.
Sharing the happy news

The next day, after a nearly sleepless night from still-overflowing euphoria, Nisa visited her parents' house to deliver that news directly — a moment she wanted to convey herself, not over the phone.
“Ma, Pa,” she said, sitting in the same living room where years ago she'd faced heavy interrogation about her relationship with Reza, now with a far warmer atmosphere. “I'm pregnant.”
Fatima immediately stood, embracing her daughter tightly, tears of happiness flowing heavily. “Alhamdulillah, Nis! Oh Allah, finally!”

Ahmed, sitting in his chair, was silent briefly before smiling widely — a sincere smile rarely seen since the tension-filled times years ago. “Father's first grandchild,” he said, his voice trembling with emotion he rarely showed openly. “Alhamdulillah, Nisa. Father is happy for you.”
That moment, however simple it looked, felt like a sweet closing to the long journey of their family's reconciliation — real proof that time and sincerity could heal wounds that once felt so deep.

Reza, who followed a few minutes later, was welcomed with warm embraces from both his in-laws — something far different from the cold reception years ago when he was first introduced as their daughter's “special friend.”
“Take good care of Nisa, Reza,” Ahmed messaged, patting his son-in-law's shoulder with full warmth. “And take care of Father's grandchild too.”
“Definitely, Pak,” Reza answered firmly, his smile never leaving throughout that visit.
Adjusting the rhythm

That pregnancy, though welcomed with overflowing happiness, also brought a series of decisions they had to make together. The tour schedule that all this time had been the pulse of their lives now had to be reconsidered carefully.

“I don't want to force myself, Za,” Nisa said in a serious conversation with Jason and Reza in their work room, her hand unconsciously already beginning to habitually rest on her belly not yet showing any change. “But I'm also not ready to stop music completely.”

“We can arrange it, Nis,” Jason, though initially a bit panicked thinking about its impact on the neatly arranged schedule, quickly adapted. “Reduce international tours for a while, focus on local events not too physically demanding. Last trimester, we can pause completely.”

Reza gripped his wife's hand tightly throughout that discussion, decision after decision they made together with mature consideration — Nisa's health and their future child always becoming the top priority above everything, including above the career ambition they'd built with great difficulty all this time.

The pregnancy news, once announced in a limited way to their close circle, was welcomed with overflowing warmth from Reza's family far abroad, from several foundation staff who had become close to them, and from fellow musicians who had long been their work colleagues. Nisa found herself not lacking warmth at all — though she realized, in a calm way and without regret, that circle no longer included a close best friend figure like before in her teenage years. Somehow, since her marriage, her life path and those old people slowly parted on their own — and strangely, she never truly felt loss because of it. Her life, with Reza and the music filling her soul, felt already full in its own way.

Several months later, in one of their routine visits to the obstetrician, the ultrasound screen displayed a blurry image that for a layperson might be hard to understand, but for Nisa and Reza felt like the most real miracle they'd ever witnessed.
“Want to know the gender?” their obstetrician asked, smiling friendly.
Nisa and Reza looked at each other, smiling in unison. “Yes, Doc,” Nisa answered, gripping Reza's hand tighter.
“A boy,” the doctor said, pointing to a small area on the screen that was the proof. “Healthy, development matching gestational age.”
Reza kissed his wife's forehead, his eyes teary. “Our son, Nis.”
That night, on the drive home, they both began discussing names — a long list they'd secretly compiled over the past few weeks, each with meanings they considered seriously.
“I like a name that's simple but meaningful, Za,” Nisa said, opening notes on her phone containing dozens of names they'd crossed off one by one over weeks. “Doesn't need to be too complicated.”
“Agreed,” Reza nodded, his eyes still looking at the ultrasound screen printed in his hand. “How about… Alexander? But called Alex daily.”
“Alex,” Nisa repeated that name slowly, tasting its sound on her tongue. “I like it. Simple, but sounds strong.”
“Alexander Satria,” Reza continued, trying to arrange his full name. “Or… do you have a middle name idea?”

Nisa was silent briefly, thinking about something she'd long kept in her heart since this pregnancy began. “How about there's an element of your name in there too, Za? So he carries both his parents' names.”

They spent the rest of the drive home that night arranging various combinations, laughing together every time one of them proposed something that sounded strange, until finally a name felt most right in both their hearts: Alex, a name that was simple but full of meaning, which they would bring home with them eight months later.
The final months

According to their agreement, Nisa began reducing her stage schedule gradually entering the third trimester, leaving only a few local performances not too physically demanding, before finally stopping completely two months before the estimated delivery.

Reza, on the other hand, began dividing his time more carefully — still carrying out his professional commitments but always making sure he could come home on time, always there to accompany every pregnancy checkup, every night when Nisa began having difficulty sleeping because of her increasingly large belly.
“You don't have to keep guarding me, Za,” Nisa said one night, though it was clear from her tone of voice how she appreciated her husband's full attention. “I know you still have work.”
“Nothing is more important than this, Nis,” Reza answered firmly, his hand gently stroking his wife's belly where small movements from within were beginning to be felt. “Nothing.”
December 14, 2029

The first contraction came toward midnight, waking them both from restless sleep. Nisa shook Reza's shoulder as he was still half asleep, her voice tense holding back pain beginning to spread. “Za… Za, wake up. I think it's time.”

Reza immediately woke fully, adrenaline defeating his sleepiness within seconds. The bag they'd prepared weeks earlier was immediately grabbed, and within less than twenty minutes, they were already driving on Jakarta streets that thankfully were still relatively empty at that early hour.

At the hospital, the following hours passed in a combination of pain, tension, and prayers Nisa ceaselessly raised between every increasingly intense contraction. Reza didn't leave his wife's side for a second, her hand gripped tightly, words of encouragement continuously flowing from his lips though his own voice began going hoarse holding back emotion and worry mixed together.
“You're strong, Nis. You're the strongest I've ever known,” he whispered repeatedly, wiping the sweat on his wife's forehead. “A little longer, Darling. A little longer and we'll meet him.”

And finally, amid the combination of pain, fear, and hope mixed together, the first cry of a baby boy broke the delivery room's silence — a sound that, though only lasting a few seconds before that crying subsided in his mother's embrace, would keep echoing in both their memories forever as the most beautiful sound they'd ever heard.
Reza, who stood beside his wife throughout the delivery process, his tears flowing without him realizing as the nurse placed that tiny baby on Nisa's chest, exhausted but shining with happiness.
“Hello, Alex,” Nisa whispered, her voice trembling with unrestrained emotion, looking at the small face that had just opened its eyes for the first time to the world. “Welcome, Darling.”
Reza knelt beside the bed, kissing his wife's forehead, then carefully kissing their son's forehead still red and wrinkled. “We did it, Nis. We have a family now.”

Several hours later, after Nisa and little Alex both slept soundly in the quiet ward, Reza sat alone in the chair beside the bed, looking at the faces of the two people who were now the center of his whole life. He took out his phone, typing a short message to his parents abroad — happy news they'd long awaited.
The reply came within minutes, full of emojis and expressions of gratitude, another reminder of how far the reconciliation journey they'd traveled as a family over the past years.

Outside the hospital window, Jakarta that night was still glittering as usual, completely unaware that in one of its rooms, a new life had just begun — a child who, though not one of them knew at the time, would grow up witnessing his parents travel a journey far bigger than just a music stage, toward something that would change not only their family's life, but also the lives of millions of other people in the country they loved.

Something more than just music.”

7: Reza & Nisa's Apartment, Jakarta — Several days later

That night, for the first time since marrying, Nisa decided to tell something she'd kept tightly all this time — even more tightly than the EDM CD collection she once hid in her locked bedroom drawer.

She and Reza had just finished praying Isha in congregation, sitting together on the prayer mat still spread in their apartment's living room, a calm atmosphere enveloping after a long day. Nisa had performed istikharah over the last few nights, seeking certainty of heart in her own way, and tonight she felt her heart was steady enough to finally open the secret she'd long buried.
“Za,” she said slowly, sitting cross-legged facing her husband, “I want to tell you something. Something I've never told anyone in full.”
Reza looked at her, feeling a different seriousness in his wife's tone of voice. He set down the mushaf he'd just been reading, giving her his full attention. “I'm listening, Nis.”
“I want to become President, Za,” Nisa began, her voice slightly trembling but firm. “Not a desire that just appeared. This has been churning for a very long time, I just buried it deep.”
Reza fell silent, waiting, not showing excessive shock even though inside his heart, that admission felt far bigger than he'd guessed.

“Do you remember that time, in our studio, the first night I dared to seriously learn DJing?” Nisa continued, her eyes gazing far. “I told you, it felt like finally two sides of me met. What I didn't fully tell you then, was how deep the wound was that came from the separation of those two sides for years.”

She sighed long before continuing. “My family completely forbade it, Za. Not just disagreed — truly forbade, in a harsh way, until I had to hide like a thief in my own house just to listen to music I liked. I still remember the feeling, every time I danced a little alone in my room while listening to a song, I had to immediately stop if I heard footsteps outside the door. It felt like there was something purest and most alive in me, that I had to keep killing myself, over and over, just because I'm a woman, and because that was considered improper.”
Reza gripped her hand, feeling the burden in every word coming from his wife's mouth.

“Now, every time I'm on stage, Za,” Nisa continued, her voice beginning to tremble with overflowing emotion, “every time I feel thousands of people moving together, uniting through the same music, I only truly realize how much was taken from me before. This isn't just about a hobby, Za. This is about the most basic right to feel alive, to feel free to move, free to express, without having to ask anyone's permission, without having to fear being judged.”

She fell silent a moment, her eyes teary. “And that's not everything, Za. There's another part of this story far heavier, that I'm not ready to tell now. But let me just say first — that prohibition about music wasn't the only way they tried to control my life back then.”
Reza straightened his body, his brows furrowed with worry. “Nis…”
“Not now, Za,” Nisa gripped his hand, calming him. “I promise, I'll tell everything. But it takes time for me to gather the courage to open all that.”
“Then why did you never tell me this side before, Nis? About how harshly they forbade you back then?”

Nisa sighed long, gathering courage to continue. “Because I buried that dream, Za, as deeply as I buried that wound. As I got older, I started seeing what the political world is really like — full of compromise, full of people who forget why they started fighting, full of corruption that even good people sometimes get pulled into. I was afraid that if I entered there, I'd become like them. I was afraid my idealism would fade, or I'd actually become part of the problem I originally wanted to solve.”

She fell silent a moment, before continuing in a softer voice. “So I chose the safer path. Ordinary office work, a calm life, nothing complicated, not exposing myself to that world I feared. Until this music came, and until you came, Za. Reza gripped his wife's hand tightly, letting silence briefly before speaking, making sure his words came out carefully and full of consideration.

“Nis,” he said finally, “I understand now why you've looked restless these last months. This isn't just about empathy for people you met on tour. This is about something far deeper that's trying to find a way out.”

“I don't think you're crazy,” Reza shook his head firmly. “Actually I think, maybe this is what has to happen. Do you remember, when we started getting serious about this music? Nisa looked at her husband, tears beginning to pool at the corner of her eyes — not tears of sadness, but something more complex, a mix between relief at finally being able to share this secret, and fear of what might happen if she truly pursued it.
“But Za, this isn't just about learning a new skill. This is about entering a truly different world. A world I fear will change me into someone I hate.”

“That's why,” Reza gripped both her hands, looking deep into her eyes, “if that's truly a calling for you, Nis, we won't enter there carelessly. That night continued with a long conversation, flowing from one topic to another — about Nisa's specific fears toward the political world, about how she imagined she could be different from politicians she'd all this time criticized inwardly, about what she needed to learn and prepare if she truly wanted to step in that direction someday.

That afternoon, after Reza left for the studio for a long-scheduled production session, Nisa sat alone in their small work room, opening the notebook that for weeks had held the stories from their tour. Outside, the afternoon sun began lowering on Jakarta's western horizon, reflecting golden light onto their apartment window — a symbol that, though Nisa didn't consciously realize it at the time, seemed to mark the end of one chapter in her life, and the beginning of another chapter that would take her, step by step, toward a destiny far beyond anything she'd ever imagined.
