Reza embraced his wife tightly, letting Nisa cry on his shoulder for a while before finally speaking, his voice now full of understanding far deeper than a husband's mere sympathy.

“Nis, listen to me,” he said, holding his wife's face with both hands, looking straight into her eyes. “I understand now. Truly understand. This isn't just about you nearly being arranged into marriage. This is about your most basic right as a human being nearly seized by people who should have guarded you most. And that… that didn't just happen to you, Nis. That happens to millions of other women out there, every day, and they don't have the luxury of telling anyone, let alone fighting to escape like you.”

He sighed long, his own eyes beginning to tear — something rare for Reza. “I'm extraordinarily grateful you managed to escape, Nis. I'm grateful Allah brought us together, at the right time, at the right point. But now I also understand, why the news about that Sukamaju girl stuck so deep in your head. That's not just empathy, Nis. That's you, a version who wasn't as lucky as you.”

Nisa fell silent a moment, wiping her tears, before continuing in a slightly different tone — no longer as heavy as before, but still holding its own pain. “There are two more things I've realized lately, Za. Not as devastating as about Father, but still… painful.”
“What are they, Nis?”

“Mother,” Nisa sighed. “I only just realized, at that time Mother was involved too, Za. Not just staying silent when Father threatened. Mother also agreed at one point, helped persuade me to accept that arranged marriage. I was too focused on Father's anger before, until I didn't truly realize how much Mother was part of that. I can't fully trust Mother like before anymore, Za. Not that I hate her, but there's a distance I can't lie about to myself anymore.”
Reza nodded slowly, listening carefully.

“And one more,” Nisa continued, her eyes gazing far, “Salma. My best friend from high school. I only realized lately, it's so strange she could agree that quickly when I told her about you before. She was my religious study friend, Za, whom I knew was very devout. But she almost never asked deeper, almost never objected at all. And after I married… she slowly disappeared just like that. No drama, no fight. Just distancing, slowly, until finally we never truly talked again.”
“Do you think about why?” Reza asked softly.

“I don't know for sure, Za,” Nisa shook her head. “Maybe she felt uncomfortable with my life choice, but didn't dare say directly. Maybe there was another reason I don't know. But what I know, I stopped waiting for her to come back long ago. And strangely, I'm fine, Za. I don't feel a big loss. This music, you, the life I've built now — all of that is already enough for me. Maybe that's Allah's way of showing, I don't need validation from people who can't truly accept me as I am.”

Reza gripped his wife's hand, looking at her with a mix of admiration and emotion. “That's extraordinary strength, Nis. Not everyone can be that strong, letting go of people who should be close, but staying whole and happy without them.”

“Maybe that's actually the proof, Za,” Nisa smiled a little amid her remaining tears. “Proof that I'm truly free now. Free even from the need to be validated by people I once thought were irreplaceable.”

“Za,” Nisa continued after her crying subsided, her voice now calmer but filled with determination hardening like steel, “I survived. I was lucky. But how many women out there aren't as lucky as me? Who don't have a Reza to fight for? Who don't have the courage I somehow got from somewhere back then?”

She rose from her husband's embrace, walking to the window, looking at Jakarta's night darkness stretching before her. “I think about this continuously, Za. About how these women — they're the source of life. They're the ones who give birth to the next generation, who nurture, who become the family's foundation. But they themselves are never given the right to recover, to be safe, to be at peace, even within their own families. They're sacrificed, made scapegoats, their energy stolen for free by people around them who should protect them.”
She fell silent a moment, as if rearranging something that had long spun in her head, trying to place it in the right order for the first time.

“Za, I have to be honest about something,” she continued, turning to look at her husband. “All the stories I heard on tour — layoffs, illegal levies, damaged roads, Budi who isn't in school yet — all of that made me sad, made me angry at a failing system. But if I'm honest with myself, that's not what moves me most deeply, Za. What's deepest actually comes from my own experience. From nearly being forced into marriage. From years not being given the right to simply love music, chase my own passion, just because I'm a woman.”
Reza listened carefully, letting his wife weave a thought she was clearly articulating this clearly for the first time.

“If you think about it,” Nisa continued, “all the other problems I heard on tour are important, Za. Truly important. But if this country fixes all that — economy, infrastructure, corruption — while its own women still have their rights seized, still aren't given freedom to be themselves, to be safe in their own homes… that's futile, Za. Because women are the ones who will later guard and nurture every household, every next generation. If the source itself isn't guarded, isn't empowered, everything else will keep being fragile, keep being damaged from its roots, no matter how good the economic or infrastructure numbers look on paper.”

“So this is the most primary for you,” Reza said slowly, beginning to fully understand the order of priority that had just formed clearly in his wife's head. “Not what you heard first. But what's deepest.”

“What's deepest,” Nisa nodded firmly. “Everything else — layoffs, corruption, infrastructure — will still be part of my struggle later. But if I have to be honest about what moves me most, what makes me unable to stay silent anymore, it's this, Za. This is about women. This is about me.”
Reza stood, approaching his wife, listening carefully to every word coming from her mouth — words sounding like a dam finally bursting after years holding back a current too big.

“This isn't just about one girl in one village, Za,” Nisa continued, her voice trembling with overflowing emotion. “This is systemic. This is embedded from generation to generation, in the heads of parents, of fathers, about how a daughter should be — obedient, compliant, becoming an asset that can be 'secured' through the 'right' marriage. And the most painful, Za, this is so often wrapped in religious language, with the reason 'this is best according to teaching,' when that's not the actual teaching. That's culture, that's ego, that's fear of what people say, dressed in religion's clothes so it looks legitimate.”

“I remember Ustaz Rahman's words back then, Za,” Nisa looked at her husband. “He said, religion should liberate, not confine. But in reality, how many parents use religion's name to justify decisions that are actually just about control, about their own ego? How many daughters have their right to learn, to choose their own life path, to feel safe even in their own home, seized in the name of something they call 'sacred,' when that's far from actual sanctity?”

Reza fell silent a long time, digesting his wife's words flowing with a power he'd never witnessed before. “Nis,” he said finally, “I understand now. This isn't just about your empathy for others. This is your own wound not yet fully healed, which now finds its form to become something bigger.”

“Maybe,” Nisa nodded slowly, tears still wetting her cheeks but her eyes now blazing with determination different from the restlessness she'd been feeling all this time. “But Za, I don't want this to just be a wound I keep to myself. I want this to become strength. I want every woman who experiences what I nearly experienced, to know they have the right to say no. That their bodies, their lives, their futures, aren't anyone's property to be decided without their consent.”

She looked at Reza straight on, her voice now firm without the doubt that usually colored their previous conversations about this dream. “I was afraid before to chase the dream of becoming president because I was afraid the political world would change me. But now I realize, Za — if I keep staying silent, if I keep letting that fear control me, I'm the same as the system that all this time stayed silent seeing these women's suffering. I can't be like that anymore.”
“So this is no longer about 'maybe someday,' Nis?” Reza asked softly, though he could already guess the answer from his wife's gaze.

“No longer, Za,” Nisa answered firmly, for the first time since that dream awoke a few months ago, without a shred of doubt in her voice. “I can't keep waiting for the right time, can't keep waiting until I feel ready enough. Because every day I wait, there's another woman losing her rights, losing her dreams, even losing her life. I have to start moving, Za. Now.”

The night grew later, but sleep felt impossible for both of them. Nisa took her notebook, opened a new page, and began writing something that felt like a crystallization of everything that had been churning within her over the last months.

“Za,” she said, while continuing to write, “I feel there are three most fundamental things seized from these women. First, the right over their own bodies — forced to marry, forced to have relations with someone they might not even accept, forced to have children from someone who isn't their choice. That… that's like a form of violence planned from birth, Za. Not a spontaneous incident, but already embedded in how their parents think since that child was still a baby.”
Reza listened seriously, letting his wife weave her thoughts without interruption.

“Second,” Nisa continued, “the right over their souls. The trauma they bury, the fear they keep alone, without anyone telling them that feeling is valid, that they may be angry, may be sad, may refuse. I experienced that, Za. For years I thought I had to comply, had to accept, because that's what's 'good' for a daughter.”
“And the third?” Reza asked softly.

“The right over knowledge,” Nisa looked at her husband. “The right to learn, to know the truth about their own bodies, about their rights, about what religion actually teaches versus what's just culture wrapped in religion. Many of them are never given access to that knowledge, Za. They're raised in deliberate blindness, so they're easier to control.”

Reza looked at his wife with deepening admiration. “Free body, free soul, free knowledge,” he murmured, repeating the three things his wife had just spoken, as if trying to feel the weight of each word. “That… that's a really strong framework, Nis.”

Nisa fell silent a moment, looking at what she'd just written, as if only realizing the power of her own words. “I don't know what this will become later, Za. But I feel this is important. This isn't just about me becoming president. This is about a philosophy that must become the foundation of whatever I do next.”
That same night

After closing her notebook, Nisa asked Reza to go out briefly — needing fresh air, needing space to let everything she'd just written settle. They drove without a definite destination, tracing Jakarta streets beginning to empty late at night.

In the car during that drive, Reza drove in a long silence, his mind clearly wrestling with something big. Nisa noticed her husband's jaw still slightly tense, his eyes occasionally gazing far beyond the road ahead of them.
“Za? What are you thinking about?”
Reza didn't answer immediately. He pulled their car over in an empty parking area near a city park, turned off the engine, and turned fully toward his wife.

“Nis,” he said, his voice full of firmness Nisa had never heard before, even on their most emotional nights, “I've listened to everything. Your story, the three pillars you just formulated, everything. And I want to say something important.”
Nisa looked at him, waiting.

“I don't just want to 'support' you anymore, Nis,” Reza continued. “That word sounds too passive for what I feel now. I want to go all-in. Fully. I want to become the person who understands your struggle most, besides yourself. Not just standing beside you — I want to help build this together, from the most basic foundation.”
“What do you mean?”

“I've been thinking about this the last few days,” Reza continued, his enthusiasm beginning to burn. “Our music will still run, that's still our main income source for now. But I also want to start exploring business, Nis. Not to leave music, but to build bigger, more stable resources, that we can use to support whatever you need going forward — whether that's a foundation, a campaign, or whatever form it takes later. I want to become a sturdy financial foundation for all this.”
Nisa looked at her husband, stunned by the earnestness radiating from his eyes. “Za, this… this is a big decision.”

“I know,” Reza gripped her hand tightly. “But listen to me first, Nis. This isn't just about me wanting to help you. This is also about something I myself now believe, from the deepest depths of my heart.” He took a long breath, gathering words that had been churning within him throughout the drive home.

“Women are the main source of life energy and love in this universe, Nis. That's undeniable. You're the ones who conceive, who give birth, who become the first foundation of every human who has ever lived on this earth. If women in this world are damaged, silenced, not given equal rights and opportunities to men, then this whole world is damaged too, Nis. This universe is damaged. The descendants who will be born after us are damaged. I only truly understood that, fully, tonight.”
Tears again pooled in Nisa's eyes, this time not tears of sadness, but such deep emotion hearing her husband articulate a conviction even more firm than she'd ever spoken herself.
“Za…”

“And Nis,” Reza continued, his voice softening but not losing its intensity, “I also want you to know one more thing. Since you started daring to be your whole self — from starting to dare to DJ in public, to now daring to open your deepest wound — I've seen you become more alive, Nis. More free, more radiant, in a way that makes me myself feel more alive. Every time you're on stage, moving, playing music with your whole soul, I feel something hard for me to describe in words — like I'm lighting up along with you.”

He gripped both Nisa's hands, looking at her with an earnestness that warmed that whole dim car space. “So if you ask why I want to go all-in this far for your dream of becoming president — it's not just because I'm a good husband, Nis. But because I myself feel my life, my meaning, my purpose, somehow keeps growing every time you become more free to be yourself. You give me a source of energy I never knew I needed. So allow me to be part of this struggle, Nis. Not just as a husband supporting from behind, but as someone who lives and moves along with you, step by step.”

He fell silent a moment, as if only realizing something bigger than his own personal experience. “And Nis, I'm starting to think, this isn't just about me and you. Look at the men around us — however successful they are, however rich they are, as soon as they don't have a stable woman figure in their lives — whether that's a wife, mother, or whoever — they waver so easily, burn out, even lose direction. I felt it a little myself, when I didn't know you yet, when the only thing filling my life was music and the stage.”
“What do you mean?” Nisa asked softly.

“I mean, this isn't just about justice for women alone, Nis — though that's already more than enough reason,” Reza continued, his voice full of conviction that had just settled. “This is about a far more fundamental balance. If the women in this country aren't empowered, aren't given room to be independent and whole as themselves, that doesn't just damage them. That damages the balance in every home, in every family — including for men who, realized or not, need that figure to still have footing.”
Nisa looked at her husband, stunned by the depth of thought she'd just heard. “Za, that's… that's such a deep insight.”
“I only realized it tonight, Nis,” Reza smiled a little. “Because of you.”

Nisa could no longer hold back her tears. She embraced her husband tightly, drowning in an embrace that felt like the sturdiest anchor she'd ever had in her life. “Thank you, Za,” she whispered between sobs now mixed with overflowing gratitude. “Thank you for truly understanding. Not just listening, but truly understanding.”
“Always, Nis,” Reza whispered, kissing the top of her head. “Always.”

That night, arriving home, something between them felt different — deeper, fuller, than previous nights. After everything they'd shared that night, after the last wall that had all this time partitioned part of Nisa finally collapsed fully before her husband, there was a kind of new closeness growing between them — not just emotional closeness, but also something more comprehensive, more whole, covering every side of their marriage.

Nisa herself realized that the next morning, smiling to herself while preparing breakfast, remembering how full the gratitude was that flowed from her that night — not only because Reza listened, but because Reza was truly present, in every sense, for a woman who for the first time felt fully seen, understood, and loved as she was. There was a kind of unwritten law of balance in their marriage — the more whole and free Nisa felt being herself, the fuller too the love she poured back to her husband, in all its forms.

Reza, leaning in the kitchen doorway that morning watching his wife humming softly while cooking, smiled to himself remembering the night before — and agreed inwardly with what he'd long suspected but only truly fully understood now: that a woman's happiness and freedom doesn't only heal herself, but also flows back, multiplied, to everyone who loves her sincerely.

That night, something long churning within Nisa finally found its whole form — no longer just directionless restlessness, but a clear mission, rooted in her own personal wound but grown far beyond the boundaries of her personal experience, transforming into a calling to fight for the rights of millions of other women throughout the country who weren't as lucky as her.

Reza gripped both his wife's hands, looking into her eyes with admiration mixed with the natural worry of a husband witnessing his wife prepare to step into a field far heavier than anything they'd ever faced together.
“I'm so proud of you, Nis,” he whispered. “And I'll be beside you, step by step, to wherever this journey takes us.”

Outside the window, Jakarta that night remained the same as usual — glittering, busy, unaware that inside one of its apartments, a fire that had long smoldered in silence, had now blazed with a power that could no longer be extinguished.
9: Reza & Nisa's Apartment, Jakarta — Several days after the conversation in the car

Since that night in the car, there was a clearly felt change in Reza — not a dramatic startling change, but a new calm, a kind of certainty of direction Nisa had never seen before in her husband. She found Reza increasingly often sitting in their work room late at night, no longer tinkering with music tracks as usual, but reading business articles, watching educational videos about investment and financial management, noting something in a small notebook he'd just bought.

“Za,” Nisa finally asked one night, finding her husband seriously staring at a laptop screen displaying a complicated spreadsheet full of numbers completely foreign to her, “what have you been doing lately? This isn't music production software.”

Reza turned, slightly startled, then smiled awkwardly. “This… this is the time for me to tell something deeper, Nis. You know I studied economics at UI — you've known that from long ago, from the start we got close. But there's part of that story I've never told you fully, even after nine years we've been together.”

Nisa nodded, recalling their light conversations years ago in their early dating days — Reza had indeed briefly mentioned his university background, something that at the time felt like an ordinary biographical detail, no more important than the fact that he was an only child or that he'd once joined the high school basketball club. “Yes, I remember you once said that. But you indeed never told the details. Why is that?”

Reza sat beside her, curious about his wife's tone of voice that now actually made him increasingly certain there was something deeper he needed to share — not merely the fact that he'd once studied economics, but the whole emotional burden that had all this time accompanied that fact.

Reza rose from his chair, walked to the cabinet in the room's corner, and took out an old plastic folder from the top shelf — something clearly rarely touched, covered in thin dust indicating long untouched.
He opened it, took out a sheet of paper already yellowed at its edges, and handed it to Nisa.
A diploma. Bachelor of Economics, University of Indonesia, 2018.

Nisa stared at that paper — not with shock at the fact that this diploma existed, because she indeed already knew that, but with deep curiosity seeing her husband so seriously showing something that all this time had been kept neatly, far from anyone's reach, including her own. “Za… I know you studied economics. But I've never seen the diploma directly like this. Why did you keep it this neatly, until it's this dusty?”

Reza sat back in the chair beside his wife, placing that diploma on the table between them. “What I've never told, Nis, is the story behind this paper. I graduated cum laude, actually — that's a detail I never boasted about to anyone, even to you.” He smiled bitterly remembering a past he'd long buried. “My parents wanted me to become a banker, or at least work at a reputable multinational company. They'd even prepared connections for me to intern at one of the biggest investment banks as soon as I graduated.”
“Then why did you never tell details this deep, Za?” Nisa asked, repeating the kind of question she'd once asked years ago about another secret — but now feeling heavier, more personal.

“Because for me, that's part of my life I'd closed tightly, Nis. I'm DJ Rez G, not an economics graduate from UI who 'failed' to become a banker according to family expectations.” He sighed long, his eyes gazing far into times he'd long tried to forget. “As soon as I graduated, what I felt was only extraordinary emptiness, Nis. Four years I studied something I myself never truly had passion for. Music had become my soul's calling since high school — I started learning mixing at sixteen, secretly, actually the same as you before, only the difference is I didn't need to hide too much because my parents were more permissive about it, they thought it was just a teenage hobby that would disappear on its own once I became an adult.”
“But that never disappeared.”

“Never,” Reza smiled a little, but that smile slowly faded as old memories began appearing. “I still clearly remember the night I told my Mother and Father that I refused that investment bank internship offer. My father — usually a calm person, rarely losing his temper — at that time was truly furious. 'Four years, Reza. Four years we paid for your education, and you want to throw that all away to become a music spinner in a nightclub?' he said at that time. Those words still stick clearly in my head until now.”
Nisa squeezed her husband's hand, feeling the weight of the memories Reza was sharing.

“My mother was even worse,” Reza continued, his voice beginning to tremble remembering those difficult times. “She didn't get angry like Father. She was just… silent. For months. Every time I came home, she treated me like a stranger just staying over to sleep. That was far more painful compared to being scolded, Nis. It took almost a year before finally she was willing to talk normally to me again, and even after that, there was a distance that never truly disappeared until years later.”
“Why did they finally accept it?”

“When I started succeeding, Nis. Ironically like that. When the name DJ Rez G started being known, when my income started exceeding what I could get as a junior banker, they slowly started… softening. Though I know, deep in their hearts, they still hoped someday I'd 'return to the right path' professionally.” Reza laughed a little, bitterly. “That's why I never told about this diploma to anyone, including you. It felt like… admitting a failure I myself never considered a failure.”
Nisa gripped her husband's hand, listening with full attention, beginning to understand another layer of Reza hidden all this time behind the DJ identity she'd known.
“Why are you opening this diploma again now, Za?” she asked gently.

“Because if I want to truly go all-in supporting you, Nis — not just emotionally, but also practically, financially — I need more than just income from music,” Reza answered, his eyes now blazing with new enthusiasm. “Our music is already successful, alhamdulillah. But if you truly want to enter the political world someday, that needs far bigger and more stable resources — for the foundation we might build, for a campaign if it comes to that, for whatever you need going forward without us having to worry about money.”

He opened his laptop, showing the spreadsheet that had earlier startled Nisa. “I've started researching some investment opportunities, Nis. Not something reckless — I'm going slowly first, learning again from zero even though I have a foundation from university before. I want to build something solid, that can become a foundation for our future, for your big vision.”
Nisa looked at her husband with deepening admiration. “Za, this… this is a big decision. Are you sure you won't regret leaving full focus from music?”

“I'll never leave music entirely, Nis,” Reza gripped her hand tightly. “Music has become part of my soul, the same as being part of your soul. But I also realize, I have another ability I've buried all this time, the same as you burying your dream of becoming president. Maybe this is the time I too stop hiding from another part of myself.”
A week later

Reza arranged a meeting with an old friend from his university days, Yoga — who had now become one of the leading investment analysts at a prominent securities firm in Jakarta, someone who had long lost contact with Reza since both graduated and chose very different life paths.

“Rez! Crazy, how many years has it been since we met,” Yoga greeted warmly at a cafe in the Sudirman area, looking with admiration at his old university friend's success now widely known as DJ Rez G. “I still remember you were the best at macroeconomic analysis in class, then suddenly just disappeared after graduation. Turns out you became a famous DJ, crazy.”
Reza laughed a little, slightly embarrassed remembering how far their two life paths had branched. “That's how it is, Yog. Soul's calling in a different direction.”
“So now why do you suddenly want to learn investment again?” Yoga asked curiously, sipping his coffee.

Reza explained in broad strokes — without leaking specific details about Nisa's dream that was still very secret — that he wanted to build a more solid financial foundation for the future, something more than just music festival season income.

Yoga listened enthusiastically, beginning to give various practical insights about the current investment landscape — growing sectors, basic principles of portfolio management, the importance of risk diversification. Reza noted everything diligently, asking questions showing that his economics foundation, though long unused, was still firmly embedded within him.

“You're really lucky, Rez,” Yoga said at the end of their meeting, “having a strong knowledge foundation plus capital from your music success. Many people have to start completely from zero. You just have to 'wake up' again what's long been asleep.”

Those words echoed in Reza's mind throughout the drive home — a metaphor that felt fitting describing not only his newly begun business journey, but also his wife's journey awakening again a dream that had long slept within her.

That night's conversation continued until late, discussing various possibilities — what business sectors Reza might explore, how to balance between his still-running music career with his new business ambition, how all this would ultimately support the big vision beginning to form within Nisa.

“I'm thinking of starting from small-scale investment first,” Reza said, showing some notes he'd made. “Local technology that's developing, maybe some startups with real social impact, not just chasing profit alone. I want every investment I make to have benefit for many people too, aligned with what you're fighting for.”

“That sounds very you, Za,” Nisa smiled, remembering how since the beginning of knowing him, Reza always had sincere care behind all his achievements, though sometimes hidden behind his relaxed and humorous personality.

“I'm also thinking,” Reza continued, “maybe someday, we could have our own holding company. Not just for me personally, but to realize both our visions — a business with values, with impact, that can become an example that financial success and social good don't have to sacrifice each other.”

Nisa looked at her husband, her heart filled with overflowing gratitude. How lucky she was, having a partner who not only supported her dream, but also dared to reopen part of himself that had long been buried, to build something bigger together.
“I'm proud of you, Za,” she whispered, resting her head on her husband's shoulder. “The two of us… we're both learning to stop hiding, aren't we.”
Reza kissed the top of her head gently. “Likewise, Nis. Step by step, we face it together.”
A few days later, Reza decided to call his parents abroad — something he rarely did outside routine small-talk conversations every few weeks.

“Ma,” he said after brief small talk, gathering courage he'd long postponed, “I want to tell you something. I've started learning about investment again, about business. Using the knowledge I studied in university.”
There was a long pause at the other end of the phone, long enough that Reza worried the connection had cut off.

“Reza,” his mother's voice finally sounded, trembling with emotion long held back, “Mother… Mother is so happy to hear it, Son. Not because Mother ever wanted you to leave music. But because Mother knows, the knowledge you studied before was never in vain, just waiting for the right time to be used.”
Unexpected tears pooled at the corner of Reza's eyes hearing those words — a small but meaningful reconciliation with part of his past he'd long considered a wound that would never truly heal.
“Thank you, Ma,” he whispered, his voice trembling. “This… this means so much to me.”

After closing the phone, Reza sat pensively a moment in their work room, feeling a relief he hadn't felt in a long time — as if two parts of himself that for years had been separate, now began finding a way to unite again, the same as what his wife was experiencing with her big dream long buried.

Outside their apartment window, Jakarta that night remained the same as usual — glittering with millions of countless stories in every corner. But inside one of its apartments, two people who had long loved each other now found a new layer of their commitment — not only the love binding them as husband and wife, but also a shared vision beginning to form clearly, ready to guide them toward the next chapter in their extraordinary life journey.
10: Nisa and Reza's first step toward something bigger wasn't directly into the political world — that was too far, too foreign, and most importantly, not yet the time. The first step was using what they already had: a stage, and the ears of millions of people who all this time had listened to their music.

“Frequency for the Nation” — the name they chose together after weeks of discussion, for the series of charity concerts they began holding every few months, each time in a different city, each time with a different fundraising purpose as well.

“I want this clear from the start, Za,” Nisa said one night, as they designed the concept for their first event. “This isn't a stage for me to give political speeches or convey my anger about injustice. This is purely about gratitude. About sharing what we've received.”

Reza nodded in agreement. “I understand, Nis. If we start bringing a protest nuance onto the stage, that will change everything. People come to feel freedom through music, not to be indoctrinated. Let the music speak in its own way.”

That decision became a principle they held firmly at every subsequent performance — the stage remained a pure space for joy, for release, for sincere human connection through rhythm and melody. Nisa's restlessness, her anger toward systemic injustice, her determination burning since the night of confession in Chapter 8 — all of that remained tightly kept in the private realm, never leaking onto the stage.
First charity concert, Bandung

The first “Frequency for the Nation” concert was held in an open field in Bandung, with the purpose of raising funds for flash flood victims who had lost their homes a few months earlier. Thousands of people packed that field, its entry tickets entirely donated for relief funds, with Nisa and Reza themselves covering all operational costs from their own pockets.

That night's set was one of the most energetic and joyful they'd ever played — no sad or heavy nuance, even though the event's purpose was helping disaster victims. Nisa, who had now become a full leader in many parts of their set, built the crowd's energy with song choices that raised spirits, hope, and togetherness.

“Tonight,” she called to the crowd between her set, microphone in hand, “isn't about sadness. This is about us, as one big family, showing that we take care of each other. Let's celebrate this togetherness!”

Festive cheers welcomed her words. No tone of anger, no accusation toward the government or a failing system — only a sincere invitation to do good together, wrapped in the musical euphoria they mastered perfectly.

Backstage, a representative of the foundation that was their partner that night, moved witnessing the enthusiasm created. “I've never seen a fundraiser this festive and cheerful,” he said to Reza. “Usually charity events are heavy, full of tears. But this… this is different. People go home with happy hearts, not just guilt driving them to donate.”
Reza smiled proudly. “That's indeed our purpose. Goodness should be born from joy, not from guilt.”
After that Bandung concert, in a brief interview session with several media covering the event, a young journalist tried to dig further, directing questions toward a more political angle.
“Bu Nisa, many say charity concerts like this could be an initial step toward a political career. Is that something you're considering?”

Nisa smiled calmly, having already anticipated this kind of question. “An interesting question, but I think that's too far from what we're doing tonight. We're here purely because we love music, and we love this country. If there are people who need help, and we have a way to help through what we're skilled at, why not? That's the only reason. There's no hidden agenda.”
“But don't you see the potential influence you have now for bigger change?”

“The biggest influence I want tonight,” Nisa answered gently but firmly, “is to see one family in Bandung be able to have a roof over their heads again. That alone is more than enough for me tonight.”

Reza, standing beside her, added in a relaxed tone that melted the atmosphere. “Besides, I'm still too busy thinking about the next song transition to think about politics, Mas.” Small laughter broke out among the journalists, and the topic shifted back to matters around music and that night's event.
In the car on the drive home, Nisa sighed with relief. “Thanks for helping divert the conversation earlier, Za.”
“We have to be careful, Nis,” Reza reminded. “It's not yet time for people to know the actual direction. Let this track record speak first, slowly, before we open our real cards.”
Behind the scenes: Reza's increasingly crucial role

While Nisa became the face and soul of every concert, Reza took an equally important role behind the scenes — managing financial and logistical aspects with a precision that began being honed again since he reopened his economics diploma.

“Every rupiah that comes in must be accountable, Nis,” he said, showing the detailed bookkeeping system he'd designed for the small foundation they'd formed specifically to manage “Frequency for the Nation” funds. “I don't want even a small gap for people to accuse us of seeking profit from goodness.”

He worked with several independent auditors to ensure full transparency, publishing financial reports for every concert openly — a standard rarely applied by similar fundraisers in Indonesia at the time, but which became the characteristic distinguishing “Frequency for the Nation” from other similar initiatives.
“People are starting to notice this, Za,” Nisa said one day, showing an article praising their transparency. “Public trust in us is growing bigger because of this.”
“That's what's most important, Nis,” Reza answered. “That trust can't be bought. It takes time to build, but once it exists, it becomes a strong foundation for whatever we do next.”

Nights after concerts, when stage fatigue began subsiding, Reza would sit for hours in their work room, compiling financial reports with a thoroughness growing sharper over time — a skill that, though rooted in his formal education years ago, he now honed again with far more personal dedication.
“Aren't you tired, Za?” Nisa asked one night, finding her husband still awake at one in the morning, his eyes fixed on the laptop screen displaying rows of numbers.

“Physically tired, yes,” Reza smiled without shifting his gaze from the screen. “But soul-tired, not at all. This is like finding a puzzle piece that's been missing all this time, Nis. I'm finally using the knowledge I once studied for something truly meaningful, not just to chase an annual bonus at a bank.”

Nisa sat beside him, observing the small details Reza worked on — every expense category recorded neatly, every transaction receipt archived systematically, every report compiled to be easily understood even by lay donors.

“You know,” Nisa said softly, “before I thought the hardest part of all this would be my part — DJing in public, opening my identity, later maybe entering politics. But it turns out, the part that makes all this able to run properly, that's actually the silent work you do every night like this.”

Reza turned, smiling warmly. “We complete each other, Nis. You bring the soul and voice to the front of the stage, I make sure the foundation is strong behind. That's what makes all this sustainable, not just momentary euphoria.”
2032 — One year later

Within a year, “Frequency for the Nation” had held eight concerts in eight different cities, collecting funds whose amount far exceeded their initial expectations — channeled for natural disaster victims, for building schools in remote areas, for health assistance for underprivileged families.

What impressed many observers most wasn't only the amount of funds collected, but their consistency — how Nisa and Reza were always present directly at every aid distribution location, not merely transferring funds and moving on.

In a village in East Nusa Tenggara, where they distributed clean water well construction aid, Nisa crouched on the ground with the village children, laughing freely while helping them draw on paper — a moment that was recorded and became one of the most shared photos that year, not because it was deliberately staged for image-building, but because of the sincerity radiating so clearly from every one of Nisa's gestures.

“This Ibu Nisa is different,” a village head commented to a local reporter covering their visit. “Many rich people come, give aid, take photos, then go home. This Ibu Nisa asks the children's names, remembers their faces, even asks how they are at the next visit. That's different.”

Returning to Jakarta, Nisa reopened the photos from her visit to NTT, reviewing one by one the faces of the children she'd met — some netizens even commented jokingly that she was a “dream first lady candidate,” without realizing how close that joke was to a truth no one yet knew besides herself and Reza.

She smiled to herself reading those comments, before closing her phone and sitting pensively a moment. The sincerity people saw in every one of her visits — the way she remembered children's names, the way she truly cared about small details often missed by others — that wasn't something that could be faked, and she knew well where that sincerity came from: from her own understanding, without needing anyone's affirmation, of how meaningful it is to be noticed and seen fully, something she herself rarely felt before.

That awareness warmed her heart, while also becoming a reminder of how important it was to keep that sincerity pure, uncontaminated by any ambition, even the big ambition that had begun burning within her since months ago.

That night, returning from East Nusa Tenggara, Nisa and Reza sat together on the veranda of the simple lodging where they stayed, gazing at a night sky filled with stars — a rare sight they could never enjoy amid Jakarta's glitter.
“Za,” Nisa said slowly, “sometimes I think, isn't this already enough? We've helped many people through this way. Why do I still feel there's something missing?”

Reza gripped her hand, gazing at the same stars. “Because this is reactive help, Nis. We help when there's a disaster, when someone's in need. But what you're fighting for — about basic rights being seized, about a system that must change — that needs something more fundamental. Needs power to change the rules of the game from their roots, not just patching wounds that have already happened.”
Nisa nodded slowly, realizing the truth in her husband's words. “So this isn't the end of the journey. This is just… a warm-up.”

“An important warm-up, Nis,” Reza emphasized. “Every one of these concerts, every trust we build, every real track record we create — all of this is a foundation. Someday, if you truly step in a bigger direction, these people, these villages, these cities — they'll become witnesses that you're not just a politician who suddenly appears with empty promises. They've seen for themselves, for years, what you're fighting for.”
Nisa rested her head on her husband's shoulder, gazing at the sky stretching wide above them. “Thank you, Za. For always seeing the bigger picture, even when I myself sometimes get impatient.”
“That's my job,” Reza smiled, kissing the top of her head. “You bring the fire, I make sure that fire doesn't go out before its time to blaze fully.”

Above them, the stars kept twinkling ceaselessly, silent witnesses of a journey that, though its road was still long, had found a sturdy foundation to keep stepping forward — one concert, one village, one trust built at a time.
11: Two years running since that first charity concert in Bandung, “Frequency for the Nation” was no longer merely a series of occasional events — it had transformed into an official foundation with legal status, a clear organizational structure, permanent staff working full time, and partnerships with more than a dozen large NGOs throughout Indonesia.

That foundation's small office, located in a simple shophouse in the Kemang area — not far from the cafe where their first public performance took place years ago — was now filled with a dozen young staff working with enthusiasm as burning as that possessed by Nisa and Reza themselves.
“Do you still remember,” Reza said one morning, watching the office bustle from behind his work room window, “this used to be just an idea we discussed all night in our apartment?”
Nisa smiled, approaching her husband, joining in watching the staff busy preparing a new partnership proposal. “Now it's become something with its own life, hasn't it.”
A new face joins

One of the most significant recruitments for the foundation came in the middle of that year — a smart young woman named Angel Marina, a communications graduate from a well-known university, who previously worked at a large PR agency in Jakarta but felt empty with work that only revolved around commercial brand image.

“I saw how your foundation communicates to the public,” Angel said in her job interview with Nisa and Reza, “and that's so different from most other foundations. There's no impression of excessive image-building, everything is honest, transparent. I want to be part of that.”
Nisa and Reza looked at each other, both feeling something special from the young candidate before them — not merely technical competence, but also a values alignment they rarely found.
“Why did you leave a reputable PR agency to join a small foundation like ours?” Reza asked curiously.
Angel smiled with certainty. “Because I want work that lets me sleep soundly at night, Sir. Not just work that makes clients happy.”

That honest answer convinced them both. Angel was accepted for work that same week, beginning her role as communications staff — a small position that, without anyone realizing at the time, would develop far beyond this small foundation in the years to come.
A track record beginning to be reckoned with

Along with the foundation's growth, Nisa began receiving invitations far different from the world she'd known all this time — public policy seminars at well-known universities, discussion forums about bureaucratic reform, even occasionally invited as a resource person at think tank discussions attended by academics and former officials.

In these forums, Nisa never appeared as a musician who happened to be kind-hearted. She came with an identity slowly forming on its own — a social activist who happened to also be a DJ, not the other way around.

“In your opinion,” asked a moderator in a panel discussion at a state university, “what distinguishes your foundation's approach from celebrity philanthropy in general, which is often criticized as merely image-building?”

Nisa answered calmly, without a defensive tone. “I think the difference lies in consistency and depth of involvement. We don't come, take photos, then leave. We build long-term relationships with the communities we help. We're transparent about every rupiah coming in and going out. And most importantly, we listen — not determining ourselves what we think that community needs, but truly asking and listening to what they feel they need most.”

That answer, delivered with sincerity hard to fake, began building Nisa's reputation as a different figure — not merely a celebrity with a charity foundation, but someone who truly understood the complexity of the social issues she tried to address.

Not everyone in those forums immediately welcomed her presence warmly. A senior professor in public policy, Dr. Suherman, known for his skeptical attitude toward popular figures entering the academic realm, once challenged her directly in a forum.

“With all respect, Bu Nisa,” he said, his tone sharp but not rude, “what makes a musician feel she has the authority to speak about these complex social policies? This isn't merely about good intentions. This needs deep understanding of development economics, sociology, law.”
The room fell silent, all eyes fixed on Nisa, awaiting her reaction to that fairly harsh challenge.

Nisa smiled calmly, not provoked emotionally. “Your question is very valid, and I appreciate it. I'm indeed not an academic. But allow me to ask back — can deep understanding of social policy only come from lecture halls, or can it also come from years of going directly into the field, listening to hundreds of real stories from people directly impacted by the policies we've all this time discussed theoretically?”
Dr. Suherman fell silent a moment, not expecting an answer so calm yet sharp.

“I didn't come here to claim I understand more than academics like you, Sir,” Nisa continued. “I'm here precisely to learn from you and colleagues, while sharing what I see directly in the field. The combination of both, in my opinion, is what actually produces policy that's truly on target.”

That answer was welcomed with nods of agreement from most attendees, and even Dr. Suherman himself, though not fully won over, looked to have softened his attitude slightly, nodding slowly as a sign of respecting the answer given.

After that forum, several young academics approached Nisa, offering research collaboration — a partnership that would later become one of their foundation's greatest strengths: combining rich field data with rigorous academic analysis.
Program expansion

Under Nisa's direction, and with increasingly strong financial support from Reza's initial investments, “Frequency for the Nation” began developing more structured and sustainable programs, far beyond merely post-disaster emergency aid.

The newly formed Education Division began building small libraries in remote villages, working with local governments to ensure program sustainability. The Maternal and Child Health Division began providing nutrition assistance programs and free health checkups in areas with high stunting rates.

A young staff member named Bagas, who had joined since the foundation's first year as a field volunteer, had now been promoted to head of the Education Division — a journey that became one of the foundation's internal pride stories.

“I used to be just a college kid who volunteered to add experience to my CV, Bu,” Bagas admitted one day to Nisa, slightly embarrassed remembering his intention that was once not as noble as now. “But after seeing the impact directly, I can't think of this as just a career stepping stone anymore.”
Nisa smiled hearing it. “That's what I like most about work like this, Bagas. Not only changing the lives of people we help, but also changing the lives of people who get involved in it.”

However the program closest to Nisa's heart — though she'd never openly explained her reason even to her core team — was the Women's Empowerment Division, focused on economic skills training and legal literacy for young women in areas with high early marriage rates.
“Why are you always most enthusiastic when we discuss this program, Bu Nisa?” asked one young staff member of that division one day, curious but not suspicious.

Nisa smiled, answering carefully so as not to leak more than she should. “Because I believe, a woman who is economically empowered and understands her rights, has the strength to determine her own life path. That's something I think we still too rarely give to many women in this country.”

That answer, though sincere, only touched the surface of the depth that actually drove her dedication — a secret she still kept tightly, stored safely within the boundaries of her household with Reza.
A small moment that meant a great deal

One afternoon, during a visit to one of the Women's Empowerment Division programs in a small town in Central Java, Nisa met a young woman named Sri — not an ordinary program participant, but one of the facilitators who now taught sewing skills to other women in her village.

“I was almost forced into marriage before, Bu,” Sri told while showing her sewing work to Nisa, her tone of voice calm though the content of her story was heavy. “Luckily there was an empowerment program from your foundation that came into my village then, gave me sewing training, gave me small capital to start my own business. My parents finally saw I could be independent, and they canceled that arranged marriage plan.”
Nisa listened to that story with teary eyes, a similarity so close to her own story, though Sri wasn't at all aware of the resonance so deeply personal for the woman standing before her.
“Now I'm the one teaching other women here, Bu,” Sri continued proudly. “So they also have the choice I nearly didn't have.”

On the drive home to Jakarta that night, Nisa told that moment to Reza with a trembling voice. “Za, this… this is real proof that what we're doing truly changes people's lives. Not just theory, not just numbers in a report.”

Reza gripped her hand tightly. “This is just the beginning, Nis. Imagine if you had the power to make programs like this into national policy, not just our foundation's initiative with limited reach.”
Those words hung in the air, becoming a calm but certain reminder of the bigger purpose still awaiting them ahead.

That night, returning to Jakarta, Nisa sat in her work room, gazing at the large map of Indonesia that had long been pinned to the wall — a map that was once empty, but now filled with small colorful dots, marking every village and city that had been touched by their program over the last two years.
Reza joined her, bringing two cups of warm tea. “What are you doing?”

“Looking at this,” Nisa pointed to that map. “Every one of these dots, there's a face, there's a story, there's a life that changed, however small that change. But Za, this is still such a small part of all Indonesia. How many hundreds more dots haven't been touched at all?”
Reza stood beside her, gazing at the same map. “That's what makes us have to keep going, Nis. Not to stop satisfied with what's been achieved.”

“Sometimes I think,” Nisa continued, her voice soft, “what we're doing is like patching wounds one by one. So meaningful for each person touched. But the systemic wound itself, that's still there, continuously creating new wounds faster than we can patch.”

Reza gripped her hand, not needing to answer with words — both already understood well enough the same direction of thinking, a direction they both slowly but surely stepped together toward a future far bigger than merely a charity foundation, though the road there was still long and full of preparation that had to be undergone patiently.

At the end of that year, “Frequency for the Nation” had recorded more than a hundred thousand direct beneficiaries throughout Indonesia, an achievement far exceeding their initial expectations when they first held that simple charity concert in Bandung two years earlier.

However for Nisa, those numbers, though a source of pride, were only the beginning of a far longer road — a track record that, though she didn't yet fully realize it, was becoming an undeniable foundation for the big step she would take a few years later.
12: A year after his meeting with Yoga at the Sudirman cafe, Reza had transformed into a figure far different from the DJ Rez G once known only through bass pounding and stage lights. He now spent most of his time no longer in the music studio, but in a small work room he'd turned into a kind of private office — filled with financial reports, investment prospectuses, and economics books beginning to replace his DJ Mag magazine collection on the shelves.

The first real investment

After months of research and consultation with Yoga, Reza finally decided on his first significant investment — not into conventional financial instruments that were safe but without impact, but into an education technology startup founded by three fresh graduates from ITB, named EdukasiKita.

“The risk is also big, Nis,” Reza admitted honestly. “Eight out of ten startups fail. But I believe in their vision, and I believe if we want to make long-term impact, we have to dare take measured risks.”

“I just don't want to play around with money we've collected with such difficulty, Yog,” Reza answered seriously. “Especially if this will become a foundation for something bigger going forward.”

A philosophy beginning to form

In the following months, Reza began developing his own investment approach — a philosophy he slowly formulated through trial and error, long discussions with Yoga, and deep reflection about what he truly wanted to achieve through the business world.

“I don't want to be an investor who only chases the highest return, Nis,” he said one night, as they sat together reviewing their investment portfolio beginning to develop — now covering three other startups besides EdukasiKita, each operating in rural health, small-scale renewable energy, and women's SME empowerment sectors. “I want every rupiah I put there to have a story behind it. An investment with personal meaning

Among his continuously developing investment portfolio, there was one that quietly was closest to Reza's heart — a women's SME empowerment platform named BerdayaWanita, which helped women in remote areas access small business capital and basic business training.
“Why are you so interested in this one, Za?” Nisa asked one night, noticing how seriously her husband reviewed that platform's monthly report, far more detailed than his other investments.

Nisa looked at her husband a long time, her heart warming hearing that answer — another proof of how deeply Reza had internalized what all this time had been her hidden struggle. She didn't answer with words, only gripped her husband's hand tightly, letting that silence convey more than any sentence could express.
The first challenge

Not everything went smoothly. Six months after the initial investment, one of the startups Reza funded — operating in the renewable energy sector — experienced serious operational difficulties, nearly approaching bankruptcy due to management errors from its own founding team.

“What should I do, Yog?” Reza asked in an emergency meeting with his friend, his face showing worry rarely seen since he began his business journey. “I've already invested quite a large amount there.”

Yoga, with years of experience in the investment world, gave a calmer perspective. “This is part of the game, Rez. Not all investments will succeed. What's important now, you evaluate — is this a fundamental problem with its business, or just an execution problem that can still be fixed?”

After weeks of deep evaluation, involving independent consultants and thorough audits, Reza decided to maintain his investment but with conditions — restructuring the management team and more intensive mentoring from his own side.

“I don't want to give up that easily, Nis,” he said, explaining his decision to his wife. “Their vision is still good. The problem is just execution. If I pull my capital now, that will damage not only their business, but also dozens of people who've hung their lives on it.”
That decision, though risky, finally bore fruit — within one year, that startup succeeded in rising again with new, more solid management, even beginning to show stable profitability.
Amid the busyness, time for family

Between their both continuously increasing busyness — Nisa with her developing foundation, Reza with his increasingly complex investment portfolio — Alex who was now almost four years old grew into a cheerful child full of curiosity, often spending time playing around both his parents' feet as they worked from home.

“Mama, what's this?” Alex asked one afternoon, pointing toward the graphs on Reza's laptop screen with curious eyes, disturbing his father's serious work session in a way that never failed to make Reza smile.
“That's Father's, Darling,” Nisa answered, lifting her son into her lap. “Father is working.”
“Father works at what? Not playing music?”
Reza laughed a little, closing his laptop briefly to give full attention to his son. “Father still plays music sometimes, Lex. But now Father also helps people through another way.”
“Like Mama?” Alex asked innocently, remembering the visits he sometimes joined with his mother to the foundation office.

“Exactly like Mama,” Reza kissed the top of his son's head, exchanging a warm glance with Nisa across the room — a simple moment reminding them both, amid all the big ambitions slowly forming, that their small family remained the center of everything they were fighting for.
Trust beginning to build

News about Reza's different investment approach — patient, socially impactful, yet still financially meticulous — began spreading among Jakarta's business actors and young investors. Some business media began taking notice, inviting him for interviews and panel discussions about socially impactful investment.
“Pak Reza,” asked a journalist in one of those interviews, “many say your investment style is unusual by most investors' standards. What drives this approach?”

Reza smiled, answering with the honesty that had become his characteristic. “I used to be a DJ. People might not expect a former DJ could be serious in the investment world. But for me, this isn't about changing identity. This is about finding a new way to give impact, using an ability I'd long buried deep.”
“Some say your decision to maintain investment in that renewable energy startup that nearly went bankrupt was too emotional, not a rational business decision. Your response?”

“I don't agree that was an emotional decision,” Reza answered firmly but still calmly. “That was a decision considering the wider picture — not just numbers in this quarter's financial report, but long-term impact on dozens of employees and a vision I believe in. That's strategy, not sentimentality.”
“And your wife, Ibu Nisa, is she involved in these business decisions?”

“Nisa is my partner in everything,” Reza answered firmly. “We always discuss together, though the final decision in this field is usually mine to hold, like decisions in other fields are usually hers to hold. We complete each other.”

That interview, when it aired a few days later, received a surprisingly positive reception — not only from business circles, but also from economics academics who began citing Reza's approach as one of the early examples of “impact investing” applied seriously in Indonesia, long before that term became a trend among mainstream investors.
That night, after that interview aired, Nisa and Reza sat together on their apartment balcony, gazing at Jakarta's glitter stretching before them.
“You've come so far, Za,” Nisa said, resting her head on her husband's shoulder. “From a DJ who was once afraid to open his own diploma, now an investor invited for business media interviews.”
“We've both come far, Nis,” Reza corrected gently. “You've also come far from the woman who once secretly listened to EDM in her room.”

Nisa smiled, gazing at the night sky beginning to fill with stars, though not as clear as those they'd once seen in East Nusa Tenggara. “Sometimes I think, all this foundation we're building — my foundation, your business — this is all like preparation for something bigger, isn't it?”
Reza gripped her hand tightly, not needing to ask further what his wife meant — they both already understood well enough the direction slowly but surely beginning to form between them.
“Every one of these steps is important, Nis,” he answered. “We're no longer just building a career or a foundation. We're building a foundation for something far bigger than all that.”
“Sometimes I'm afraid, Za,” Nisa admitted honestly, her voice softening. “Afraid this foundation will never be strong enough for what I imagine ahead.”

“A strong foundation isn't built overnight, Nis,” Reza calmed her, kissing her forehead. “We've started from the right point — slowly, but rightly. Every foundation that grows, every startup we succeed in supporting, every trust we build from zero — those are all bricks that, one by one, will become a foundation sturdy enough for whatever awaits us later.”

In the distance, Jakarta city lights kept twinkling ceaselessly, silent witnesses of two people who, step by step, were building a foundation for a journey that would take them far beyond anything they'd ever imagined when they first met at a The Corrs concert years ago.
13: The turning point came from news that shook the entire country: a food aid fund corruption scandal amid a national food crisis, involving high ministry officials who were supposed to be responsible for distributing aid to millions of poor families.
