A few days later, when Nisa shared her idea in a limited way with several close foundation advisors, one of them — a former senior bureaucrat who had long helped with the foundation's legal affairs — showed honest doubt.

“Bu Nisa, with all respect,” he said in a small meeting, “if the ultimate goal is indeed in the direction I suspect, usually the path taken is formal education, conventional political networks, not… a music tour around the provinces.”

Nisa smiled calmly, not offended by that doubt. “I understand your concern, Sir. But consider, how many leaders rise through that conventional path, but turn out never truly understanding their people? How many good policies on paper fail totally as soon as they're implemented, because whoever made that policy never truly stood among the people who would be impacted by it?”

She continued, her voice growing firmer. “I'm not saying formal education isn't important. But for me personally, my most effective way of learning and most honestly connecting with other people is through music. That's been proven for years. I believe, if I want to truly understand this country wholly — not just from statistics — I have to go directly, in the way most natural for me.”
The advisor fell silent a moment, considering that answer, before finally nodding respectfully. “An unusual approach, Bu. But I'm beginning to understand its logic.”

“I also want to bring the foundation along,” Nisa continued, that big plan increasingly complete in her head. “Every city, every village we visit, we don't just perform. We also assess local needs, we distribute appropriate aid, we listen directly to what they need, not what we think they need.”
Adjusting family life
That big plan, like other big decisions, required significant adjustment to their family life. Alex who was still small became the main consideration in arranging the new tour schedule.
“I don't want this tour to make Alex feel abandoned, Za,” Nisa said, a mother's worry clearly radiating from her face.

“We can arrange it, Nis,” Reza calmed her. “Not every trip has to be nonstop without breaks. We can make a more humane rhythm — a few weeks traveling, a few weeks home, so Alex still has a stable routine at home. And sometimes, if possible, he can come with us, feeling directly too this country's diversity from young.”
Nisa smiled hearing that suggestion. “I like that idea, Za. So he also grows up with that understanding, not just hearing stories.”

Fatima, when asked for help for moments when Alex needed to stay in Jakarta, remained willing to help though Nisa's relationship with her was now no longer as warm as before — a complexity Nisa chose not to think about too much, just accepting it as it was for the stability her son needed.
A name for the big journey

After weeks of designing the concept, route, and logistics with the small team they'd begun forming — including Angel who enthusiastically helped design a communication strategy for this big journey — they finally agreed on a name: “Nusantara Bersuara Tour” (Nusantara Speaks Tour).

“I like this name,” Angel said in one of the planning meetings, her eyes gleaming full of enthusiasm. “This isn't just a music tour, Bu Nisa. This is a listening tour. Nusantara that all this time has had so many voices rarely truly heard.”

Nisa nodded, her heart filled with hardening conviction. “That's exactly the meaning, Angel. I want every city, every village we visit, they feel heard. Not just entertained momentarily, then we leave.”

That plan, ambitious and never done by any musician in Indonesia on such a scale, would take Nisa and Reza — along with a continuously growing team — exploring all corners of the country over the coming years, one province after another, one stage after another, one story after another, building a connection with the Indonesian people far deeper and wider than ever achieved through any conventional means.
Alex, who heard fragments of his parents' conversation about that big plan, one afternoon asked innocently while playing on the work room floor. “Mama and Father want to travel around Indonesia?”
“Yes, Lex,” Nisa smiled, crouching to level herself with her son. “Mama and Father want to meet so many people, listen to their stories, play music with them.”
“I come?” Alex's eyes widened full of hope.
“Sometimes, Darling,” Reza ruffled his son's hair. “So you also get to know our country up close.”

Alex looked satisfied with that answer, returning focus to his toys, not realizing that his parents' simple answer just now was the beginning of a journey that would shape not only their family's future, but also a nation's future.

That night, after the planning meeting ended, Nisa stood on their apartment balcony, gazing at the large map of Indonesia that had long been pinned to her work room wall — the same map that had once made her reflect years earlier, now soon to be filled with real traces of the journey she'd just begun.
“This is just the beginning, isn't it, Za?” she whispered, looking at her husband standing beside her.

“A big beginning, Nis,” Reza kissed her forehead, both their eyes gazing in the same direction — a future that, though its road was still long and full of uncertainty, felt so clear in its direction for the first time.

In the distance, Jakarta's lights kept twinkling, witnesses of a decision that would change not only the direction of Nisa's and Reza's lives, but also the way a nation would come to know its future leader — not through speeches and campaign promises, but through beat after beat of music that had long united their hearts.
14: Medan, North Sumatra — Early 2035

The specially modified tour bus — equipped with portable sound system equipment, a small rest area, and even a mini study corner for Alex who occasionally joined the journey — drove slowly entering a small village on Medan's outskirts, far from the city bustle they usually visited during years of their music career.

This was the seventh stop of the “Nusantara Bersuara Tour” they'd been running for the last three months — starting from Aceh, tracing Sumatra's east coast, now arriving at a village not even clearly listed on any digital map.
“Are you still sure this will work, Nis?” Reza asked, looking out the bus window toward the simple village beginning to appear, wooden houses lined along the unpaved dirt road.

“I'm more sure than before, Za,” Nisa answered, her eyes gleaming full of enthusiasm that never faded though the long journey was beginning to show in her body. “Every place we visit, I learn something I would never get from any book or report.”

Reza himself, between that long journey, still had to divide his attention between the tour and his continuously developing business portfolio in Jakarta. Every time internet signal permitted, he'd take time to video call with Yoga or the management teams of the startups he funded, ensuring everything ran smoothly though he was far from the office.

“Are you sure you can juggle all this, Rez?” Yoga asked one time in a video call, slightly worried seeing his friend looking exhausted on screen, the background showing a remote village far different from the usual office atmosphere.

“I have to be able to, Yog,” Reza smiled tiredly but full of conviction. “This is part of something far bigger. I just need to make sure our financial foundation stays strong, so whatever happens going forward, we have resources to support it.”
A methodology forms

During the first three months of that journey, a pattern had formed on its own — a methodology that, though they never planned formally at the start, now became the framework they followed at every stop.

The first day at every location always began with listening — Nisa and her small team consisting of foundation volunteers would tour the village or subdistrict, sitting together with local residents, listening to their stories without hidden agendas, without cameras continuously recording. The second day was usually filled with deeper assessment — seeing directly the condition of local infrastructure, education, health, noting real needs that were often very different from assumptions made from Jakarta.

Only on the third or fourth day was the stage erected — not a magnificent stage like the big festivals they usually played, but a simple stage that could be erected even in a village field or community hall yard. The music played was also adjusted — sometimes combined with local traditional instruments, sometimes lifting local melodies rearranged with the electronic touch that had become Nisa and Reza's characteristic.

“This is no longer just a music tour, Za,” Nisa said one night, writing in her notebook that had now grown into several thick volumes containing stories, data, and reflections from every place they visited. “This is like… the most honest education I've ever received.”
The village that changed perspective

That small village on Medan's outskirts became one of the most memorable points in their tour. There, they met a young village head named Pak Hendra, who had led his village through a prolonged economic crisis due to consecutive crop failures over three years.

“We're not asking for pity, Bu Nisa,” Pak Hendra said in a meeting with the villagers, his tone full of dignity though his village's situation was clearly concerning. “We just need to be heard. Need people who truly want to know what we need, not those who've determined it themselves from afar.”

Those words embedded deeply in Nisa's mind, becoming a kind of mantra she kept remembering throughout the subsequent tour journey. That night, after the meeting with the villagers, she and her team sat together with Pak Hendra and several other community leaders, discussing concrete solutions truly suited to local conditions — not generic aid that often missed its target, but a sustainable agriculture training program designed specifically to address the specific problem that village faced.

The concert held the next night became one of the most emotional in their tour series — not because of its large scale, but because of the closeness that had been built in just a few days. The villagers, from children to elders, gathered in that small field, dancing and singing together with Nisa and Reza with sincere joy, far from the formal or awkward impression that often accompanied officials' or celebrities' visits to remote areas.
Alex experiences it too
Alex, who was now five and a half years old, joined this tour stage — a decision carefully considered by Nisa and Reza as part of their son's early education about their own country's diversity.
“Why are the houses all different, Ma?” Alex asked one afternoon, noticing the simple wooden houses in that village, far different from the luxury apartment where they lived in Jakarta.

Nisa crouched to level herself with her son, answering carefully but honestly. “Because Indonesia is so vast, Lex. People live in different places, some in big cities like us, some in villages like this. Everyone is equally Indonesian, only their lives are different.”
“They don't have houses like ours?”
“They have houses that suit them, Darling,” Reza added, also crouching beside his wife and son. “Not everyone needs a house the same as ours. What matters is they're happy and have enough.”

Alex nodded, though clearly much remained not fully understood at his young age. However moments like that, repeated at every location they visited, slowly formed an early understanding far richer about his own country compared to children his age who grew up knowing only one urban perspective.
Challenges on the road

This big tour wasn't without heavy challenges. Some locations they visited had very poor infrastructure access, forcing them to travel by land for hours through damaged roads, or even having to use small boats to reach isolated coastal villages.

“This is insane, Za,” Nisa complained one night, her body tired after a ten-hour journey through potholed roads to a remote village in inland Sumatra. “I only just realized, this is what these people experience every day just to go to the market or to school.”

“This is what makes this journey important, Nis,” Reza calmed her, massaging his wife's tense shoulders. “If we just read reports about poor infrastructure, that's abstract. But feeling it directly for ten hours, that's completely different.”

Their team also faced countless logistical challenges — sound system equipment damaged by difficult terrain, extreme weather disrupting schedules, and occasionally skepticism from village officials suspicious of the motive of their visit, thinking this was just veiled political gimmickry.

In one village they visited in inland Aceh, a subdistrict head welcomed their arrival with clearly visible coldness. “We've been visited so often by people who say they want to help, then after taking photos they just leave,” he said bluntly in their first meeting. “Sorry if I sound skeptical, Bu Nisa.”

“I won't ask you to believe just from words,” Nisa answered calmly, not offended by that honesty. “I only ask for a chance to show through action. If after we leave, you still feel this is just gimmickry, I accept that as valid criticism.”

That humble attitude, combined with the concrete training program actually implemented by the foundation team after their visit, slowly melted the subdistrict head's skepticism. Three months later, he even sent a direct message to the foundation contact, thanking them for a program that truly brought real change for his residents — small but meaningful proof that consistency could defeat even the harshest suspicion.

National media that began covering this tour journey was also split in its response. Some praised the approach considered authentic and rare, while others questioned the motive behind it, speculation about veiled political ambition beginning to appear in various online forums.
“Have you seen this, Nis?” Reza asked one night, showing an opinion article openly accusing their tour of being an “image-building strategy toward the political stage.”
Nisa read that article calmly, showing no signs of being upset. “Let it be, Za. Time will answer. If our intention is sincere, our work results will speak for themselves, not rebuttals in the media.”

That night, after the concert in Pak Hendra's village ended and the residents began dispersing with happy faces, Nisa sat alone at the edge of the field, gazing at the night sky filled with stars — a sight that always reminded her of a similar night in East Nusa Tenggara years ago, the moment when she first truly realized her deeper restlessness.
Reza joined her, sitting beside her in comfortable silence.
“Three months, seven locations,” Nisa said softly, gazing at the stars above them. “Still thirty-one more provinces we have to visit.”
“A long journey, Nis,” Reza nodded, gripping her hand. “But look at what we've gotten in just these three months. Imagine what we'll have after years.”
The next morning, before continuing the journey to the next location, Angel — who now led the tour's documentation and data analysis team from Jakarta — sent a brief report via video call.

“Bu Nisa, the numbers are extraordinary,” Angel said, her face full of enthusiasm on the phone screen. “Total already more than fifteen thousand people directly involved in these seven locations — not just watching concerts, but participating in our listening and assessment sessions. And most importantly, the community's trust level toward the aid programs we run is far higher compared to conventional methods usually used by other institutions.”
“That's not just about numbers, Angel,” Nisa answered, smiling though fatigue was still felt on her face. “That's about people who finally feel heard.”
“I know, Bu,” Angel nodded. “But these numbers are also important to show people who are still skeptical, that this approach is truly effective, not just good on the surface.”
Nisa smiled, resting her head on her husband's shoulder. “This is just the beginning, isn't it, Za?”

“The first beat of a far bigger journey,” Reza kissed the top of her head, his eyes gazing in the same direction as his wife's — the stars stretching wide above a country that slowly but surely they were beginning to know with their whole hearts, one village, one story, one beat at a time.
15: The next two years took Nisa, Reza, and their continuously growing team exploring the corners of Indonesia least touched by national spotlight — from inland Kalimantan reachable only by hours-long river travel, to small islands in Maluku whose residents rarely even saw a government official's face directly.
Every location left its own trace in Nisa's understanding of her country — a mosaic slowly but surely beginning to form a picture far more whole and complex than she'd ever imagined before.
Kalimantan — a lesson about land and identity
The journey along Kalimantan's great rivers took them to Dayak communities living far from the regency government center, most reachable only by ces boat for hours along winding rivers.
In one of those communities, they met Pak Lambertus, a customary elder who was fighting for recognition of rights over his ancestral land threatened by large-scale plantation expansion.

“This land isn't just about economics for us, Bu Nisa,” Pak Lambertus explained, pointing to the forest stretching around them. “This is our identity. Our ancestors are buried here. If this land is lost, part of who we are is lost too.”

Nisa listened carefully, realizing the issue's complexity far beyond conventional social aid frameworks — this touched agrarian law issues, indigenous community rights, and clashes of large-scale economic interests far more complicated than anything she'd faced at previous locations.

“I can't promise to resolve this now, Pak,” Nisa admitted honestly. “But I promise to carry your story, to find out more deeply about the legal framework that could help, and to keep following up even though our tour has moved on to other locations.”

That meeting became one of the most memorable for Nisa — not because the solution was simple, but because its complexity actually taught her that leading a country as large and complex as Indonesia needed understanding far beyond generic policy, but rather sensitivity to very diverse local contexts.
Papua — a lesson about patience and dignity

Their visit to a village in inland Papua became one of the most transformative points in the entire tour journey. To reach that location, they had to take a small flight followed by hours of land travel through challenging terrain, something far beyond the logistical difficulty they'd ever faced in Sumatra or Kalimantan.
There, they met Mama Yuliana, an influential woman figure in her village, who had for decades fought for educational access for girls in her region.

“We here are used to being abandoned, Ibu Nisa,” Mama Yuliana said with eyes holding years of struggle's exhaustion, but also unshakeable dignity. “Programs come and go. Promises come and go. But we stay here, keep struggling, because there's no other choice.”

Those words struck Nisa with a force different from anything she'd felt at previous locations — no longer merely empathy toward economic difficulty, but deep awareness about how systemic distrust forms from repeated experience of being disappointed by those who should serve.

“I won't promise something I can't keep, Mama,” Nisa answered honestly, gripping the old woman's hand. “But I promise, what we do here, we'll do earnestly, and we'll keep coming back to make sure it runs.”

The program they designed together with Mama Yuliana — a community-based education initiative involving local women as teachers, rather than bringing in outside teaching staff who didn't understand local context — became one of the foundation's most successful program models and was replicated in other Papua locations in the following years.
East Nusa Tenggara — returning to the place that changed everything
Their return visit to NTT, the place that had once been an important turning point years earlier in the early days of their music career, felt like closing a meaningful circle.
“Do you remember, Za, the last time we were here?” Nisa asked, standing at almost the same location as their visit years ago, the place where they helped distribute clean water well aid.
“I remember it well,” Reza smiled, his eyes gazing into the past. “That was one of the moments that made you start thinking all this wasn't enough.”

This time, they returned not merely to help, but to see the long-term impact of the intervention they'd once made — an evaluation rarely done by conventional aid programs that usually stopped as soon as a project was completed.

They found the well they'd helped build years ago still functioning well, maintained by the local community that had been trained to care for it themselves — small but meaningful proof that a sustainable approach, not merely momentary aid, truly brought lasting change.

A child who was still a toddler during their first visit had now become a teenager attending the local secondary school — a school whose condition had much improved thanks to the continuing education program the foundation ran after that first visit.
“Kak Nisa!” he called joyfully, recognizing the figure he'd once seen in his childhood. “Kak Nisa still remembers me?”
Nisa smiled with emotion, embracing that teenager. “Of course I remember you. You've grown so big now.”
Maluku's small islands — a different challenge

The journey to the cluster of small islands in Maluku brought a completely different logistical challenge — requiring them to sail using traditional wooden boats for hours among waves that were sometimes unfriendly, carrying sound system equipment that had to be protected extra carefully from seawater.

On a small island whose residents mostly depended on the sea's yield, they met a fishing community facing a real threat from climate change — continuously declining catches due to coral reef damage, storms increasingly frequent and unpredictable.

“This isn't just about economics anymore, Za,” Nisa said one night, noting seriously in her notebook after long discussion with the local fishermen. “This is about their long-term survival. If there's no intervention about this climate change, the next generation will lose a way of life that's been passed down for hundreds of years.”

That awareness expanded the scope of their foundation's programs — from merely economic and educational aid, now beginning to extend into environmental and sustainability issues, a dimension they hadn't previously touched fully in depth.
A network that keeps growing

Amid that long journey, something not explicitly planned began forming on its own — a vast network of grassroots relationships stretching from Indonesia's western tip to its eastern tip. Village heads, community leaders, local teachers, young men and women inspired by their visits — all became small nodes of a network that, though its scale wasn't yet fully realized by Nisa herself, would later become an invaluable foundation for her political journey.

“Angel,” Nisa said one time, reviewing the contact database her team had collected throughout the tour, “this is already more than five hundred community leaders from all over Indonesia who have direct relationships with us.”

“And that doesn't include thousands of ordinary residents we've met directly, Bu,” Angel added, showing an interactive map marking every location they'd visited — a map that each month became increasingly filled with new dots.

Nisa looked at that map a long time, realizing the scale of what they were slowly building — not merely a series of charity concerts or philanthropic visits, but an authentic and vast connection with the nation's own pulse, built not through speeches or campaign promises, but through real presence, beat after beat, story after story.
Alex who begins to understand

Between that long journey, Alex who was now seven years old began showing far more mature understanding about what his parents were doing, far beyond the innocent questions he'd once thrown out at a younger age.
“Ma,” he said one night in Papua, after witnessing directly Nisa's meeting with Mama Yuliana, “why doesn't Mama just give money directly to Mama Yuliana? That would be faster.”

Nisa smiled, sitting beside her son, explaining in language a child his age could understand. “Because if Mama just gives money, Lex, that only helps briefly. But if Mama helps Mama Yuliana have her own way to keep developing — like training local teachers — that will keep helping even after Mama leaves here.”
Alex nodded slowly, digesting that explanation with a seriousness that surprised Nisa. “So like… teaching fishing, not just giving fish?”
Nisa laughed with emotion, embracing her son tightly. “Exactly like that, Darling. Where did you learn that saying?”
“Taught at school,” Alex answered proudly. “But I only understood what it meant now, because of seeing it directly.”

Moments like that, repeated at various locations throughout their journey, convinced Nisa and Reza that the decision to bring Alex along on part of the tour journey — though full of logistical challenges — gave an education far more valuable than what he could get in any classroom.

That night, at the end of the second year of their journey, Nisa and Reza sat together on the veranda of a simple lodging on a small Maluku island, gazing at the sea stretching dark before them, decorated by star twinkles far brighter than any they'd ever seen in Jakarta.
“How many provinces have we been to now, Za?” Nisa asked, resting her head on her husband's shoulder.
“Nineteen,” Reza answered without needing to think long, that number having become so familiar in his head. “Nineteen of thirty-eight.”

“Halfway,” Nisa smiled, though fatigue clearly radiated from her face. “But it feels like we're just starting, Za. Every place we visit, I feel there's more and more I don't yet understand about this country.”
“That's what makes this journey valuable, Nis,” Reza kissed the top of her head. “If you already feel you know everything, that's where you stop learning.”

In the distance, the calm sound of waves blended with the rustle of night wind, becoming the backdrop of a journey that, though its road was still long, had changed Nisa's perspective on her country fundamentally — from merely an abstract concept on a map, into millions of faces, stories, and real lives that were now an inseparable part of herself.
16: Reza's decision to truly retire completely from the DJ world came after long consideration that had matured over years of tour journeys — a decision that, though heavy, felt like a natural step from the journey they'd traveled together.

His business — Reza Satria Group, which had now grown far beyond what he'd ever imagined when he first reopened his economics diploma years ago — had developed into an investment holding with a portfolio spanning education technology, renewable energy, rural health, to women's SME empowerment. Managing all that while continuing to accompany Nisa on increasingly intensive tour journeys became a challenge increasingly difficult to run simultaneously.

“I've been thinking about this a long time, Nis,” he said one night, after they returned from a tour stage in Sulawesi. “I want to retire completely from DJing. Not just reduce the schedule like we've been doing all this time, but truly stop.”
Nisa looked at him, though she'd already guessed the direction of this conversation would come, it still felt heavy hearing it spoken officially. “Za, are you sure? That's a big part of who you are.”

“Precisely because that's a big part of who I am,” Reza answered, smiling though his eyes held sincere sadness, “I want to stop while I still love it, not until I'm forced to stop because I can no longer juggle everything. And besides—” he gripped his wife's hand, “—this business needs full focus now, Nis. Especially if we want this to become a truly strong foundation for whatever awaits us going forward.”
A mature consideration

That decision didn't come suddenly, but was the result of long reflection Reza had done between tour journeys, especially after witnessing directly how great an impact could be produced through a responsible business approach.

“I see for myself, Nis, how the programs we fund through business truly change people's lives,” he explained in a deep conversation with Yoga, who had now become a kind of permanent advisor for Reza Satria Group. “EdukasiKita has reached more than a hundred thousand students in remote areas. BerdayaWanita has helped thousands of women start their own businesses. This is impact no less great than what Nisa achieves through the tour, only in a different form.”

Yoga nodded, understanding well his friend's line of thinking. “You've found your true calling, Rez. Not just being an investor seeking profit, but becoming someone who truly understands how capital can become a tool for systemic change.”

“That's why I want to go all-in now,” Reza continued with clear determination. “If I'm still half-hearted between music and business, I won't be able to maximize the impact of either. It's time I choose focus.”
A deepening reconciliation
Reza decided to inform his parents of this big decision directly, arranging a special video call far more formal than their usual routine conversations.
“Ma, Pa,” he said, gathering courage he'd long prepared, “I want to retire completely from the DJ world. I want to focus fully on business now.”
There was a long pause at the other end of the phone, reminding him of a similar pause years ago when he first announced the opposite decision — leaving the banking world for music.

“Reza,” his mother's voice finally sounded, this time filled with emotion far different from the past disappointment, “Mother is so proud of you, Son. Not because you finally 'returned to the right path' like Mother once thought. But because Mother sees you've grown into someone who knows when to change, and why.”
His father, who rarely showed emotion openly, added in a slightly trembling voice. “That diploma finally got used, didn't it, Son. Father always believed it wouldn't be in vain.”

Those words, however simple they sounded, touched something deep in Reza's heart — a closing of a circle he'd long awaited without ever truly realizing it, full reconciliation with the part of himself he'd once considered a failure, now acknowledged as an important foundation of who he was now.
The last set

They decided Reza's last set as a professional DJ would be held at a small festival in Bali — the same place, symbolically, as one of their early performances years ago before fame truly changed their lives.
There was no large-scale announcement, no specially designed media campaign. Just a simple post they prepared for the next day, written with full honesty and gratitude.

That last performance night felt different from thousands of previous performances — not because of its scale, but because of the emotional weight accompanying it. Reza stood behind the deck for the last time as a professional, his fingers dancing over the faders with a fluency honed over more than two decades.

Nisa, who that night chose to be fully a spectator rather than co-performer as usual, stood at the edge of the stage, watching her husband with teary eyes — a final tribute to the part of Reza that had brought them both to this point.

Alex, who was now eight years old, sat beside Nisa, big enough to understand how important the moment they were witnessing together was. “Is Father sad, Ma?” he whispered, noticing his father's mixed expression on stage.
“A little sad, but also proud, Darling,” Nisa answered softly, embracing her son. “Sometimes adults have to let go of something they love, to focus on other things that are also important.”
“Like when I had to stop playing one toy to focus on learning to ride a bike?” Alex asked, trying to relate it to his own experience.
Nisa laughed a little amid her emotion, kissing the top of her son's head. “Exactly like that, Lex. Just a far bigger adult version.”
At the end of the set, when the last song began to fade, Reza removed his headphones slowly, gazing at the crowd that had accompanied him throughout his music career journey.

“Thank you,” he said simply into the microphone, his voice trembling with emotion he found hard to hide. “For every night, every beat, every energy you've shared all this time. This isn't a farewell from music — music will always be in my blood. But it's time for me to step into the next chapter.”
Life after the turntable
The weeks after that last set brought adjustments that weren't always easy for Reza, though his decision had been carefully considered.

“Sometimes I still reflexively want to go to the studio, Nis,” he admitted one night, sitting in the work room now fully dominated by financial reports and investment proposals, rather than music production equipment. “It feels strange.”

Nisa gripped his hand, understanding well the complexity of emotions her husband was experiencing. “That's natural, Za. You're letting go of a big part of your identity. But you're not alone in feeling a transition like this — I felt something similar when I first dared to open my DJ identity to the public, only the direction was reversed.”
“The difference is, you found a more whole version of yourself,” Reza smiled a little. “I feel like I'm losing a piece of myself.”
“You're not losing it, Za,” Nisa emphasized gently. “You're just finding a new way to channel the same passion — making impact, making change, only the medium is different now.”

Slowly, in the following months, Reza began finding his new rhythm — pouring the creative energy he once channeled through music, now into designing increasingly innovative and impactful investment strategies, building an increasingly solid and professional Reza Satria Group team.
An increasingly sturdy foundation

At the end of that year, Reza Satria Group had officially become one of the largest social impact investment holdings in Indonesia, with a portfolio covering more than twenty startups in various sectors, employing directly and indirectly more than ten thousand people throughout the country.

It's important to understand, Reza wasn't the person who founded and ran those twenty companies himself — something impossible for one person to do however strong their energy. Every startup in his portfolio, like EdukasiKita and BerdayaWanita, was founded and run daily by their own founding and operational teams — people with technical expertise and vision in their own fields. Reza's role was as main investor: he injected capital, sat as strategic advisor or board of commissioners member in most of those companies, and ensured every fund he invested was truly used according to the social impact vision he believed in — but daily operations were fully in the hands of the founders and their teams.

However that position, though not as direct operator, still brought significant power. As main investor in dozens of companies at once, Reza's voice in board meetings, his influence on each company's strategic direction, and the vast network he built across sectors made him one of the most influential figures in Indonesia's social impact business ecosystem — a power that worked silently but really, far from the stage spotlight once identical with him.
“Za,” Nisa said one night, reviewing Reza Satria Group's annual report with her husband, “do you realize, this has become bigger than we ever imagined when we started before?”

“Very aware, Nis,” Reza smiled proudly, though fatigue clearly radiated from his face after years of hard work. “And most importantly, this is a very sturdy foundation for whatever awaits us going forward. No more worry about financial resources. We're ready, whatever form it takes later.”

Nisa rested her head on her husband's shoulder, gazing at the annual report displayed on the laptop screen — real proof of the long journey they'd traveled together, from two people who once only had dreams and courage, now becoming a couple who had built sturdy foundations on two different fronts — social and financial — both of which would become important backbones for the big chapter still awaiting them ahead.

“You know,” Nisa continued, her voice full of reflection, “sometimes I think, the two of us are like two sides of the same coin. I build a bridge to the people's hearts through music and stories. You build a bridge to their future through capital and economic opportunity. Both are equally important.”

“And both would mean nothing without the other,” Reza added, gripping his wife's hand tightly. “The trust you build through the tour, that's what makes people believe the good intention behind every investment I fund. And the financial foundation I build, that's what ensures whatever you fight for going forward has enough resources to truly materialize.”
“We're ready, aren't we, Za?” she whispered.
“We're ready, Nis,” Reza kissed her forehead. “Now we just keep going, until the time comes.”

Outside their apartment window, Jakarta that night remained glittering as usual, witness of two people who, after years of building their respective foundations diligently and with full dedication, now stood at the threshold of the next chapter in their long journey — a chapter that, though not yet fully clear in its form, felt increasingly close with every day that passed.

22: Early 2043

“Ma,” she said when the call connected, her voice still trembling from that night's emotion, “Nisa won, Ma.”
There was a brief pause before Fatima's voice sounded, filled with unhidden tears of emotion. “Oh Allah, Nisa… Mother is so proud of you, Child. So proud.”
“Thank you, Ma,” Nisa sighed, letting part of her emotional complexity flow in a gentle but honest voice. “I know our relationship hasn't always been easy lately. But I still love you, Mother.”
“Mother loves you too, Nis,” Fatima answered, her voice full of long-restrained emotion. “Whatever has ever happened between us, that will never reduce Mother's love for you.”

That brief conversation, though not fully healing the old wound that still left its mark, became a small but meaningful moment — a reminder that family relationships, however complex, still hold space for sincere love amid all their intricacy.
Midnight reflection

After the first wave of euphoria began subsiding, and most of the team had gone home to rest ahead of the busy transition days that would soon begin, Nisa and Reza sat together briefly in the room now grown quiet, Alex having fallen asleep on the sofa from exhaustion after a long night full of emotion.
“Za,” Nisa whispered, gazing at their son sleeping soundly, “our lives will never be the same again starting now, will they?”

“Never the same,” Reza nodded, gripping her hand tightly. “But one thing I promise you, Nis — whatever changes, we'll never lose who we really are. We'll never forget where we came from, and why we started this journey.”

Nisa rested her head on her husband's shoulder, gazing at Alex sleeping peacefully, her heart filled with gratitude overflowing beyond words she could express. “Nineteen years this coming October, isn't it, Za. Since we married.”
“Nineteen years,” Reza smiled, kissing her forehead. “And look at the journey we've traveled together.”

Before leaving that room, Yoga approached Reza briefly, patting his friend's shoulder with still-teary eyes. “Rez, I still remember you were once a DJ who reopened his dusty economics diploma in the cabinet. Now look, you're not only a successful businessman, but also an important part of this nation's history.”
“Wouldn't have reached here without you, Yog,” Reza embraced his friend tightly. “Thank you for always being there, from the very beginning.”
“Always, Rez,” Yoga smiled, before finally taking his leave from the room now growing quieter.

Outside the window, Jakarta that night remained glittering as usual, but for the two people sitting in that small room, that same city now felt different — no longer merely the backdrop of their lives, but part of a great responsibility they had just officially shouldered, a trust they had prepared for wholeheartedly over almost two decades of a journey full of love, struggle, and sacrifice that was never in vain.
25: October 2044

Amid the extraordinary busyness preparing the power transition — security protocols that had to be learned, a cabinet team beginning to be formed, marathon meetings with the government that would soon hand over — Nisa decided to do one last thing before officially donning her new identity as President of the Republic of Indonesia.
“Za,” she said one night, a few days before the inauguration scheduled for October 20, “I want us to go back to our studio. The small studio from before.”
Reza looked at his wife, fully understanding the meaning behind that simple request. “The studio in our old apartment?”
Nisa nodded. “I know we moved from there long ago. But I heard, that unit is still empty, no one has occupied it again since we moved years ago.”
Alex, who heard his parents' conversation, became curious too. “Can I come, Ma?”
Nisa and Reza looked at each other a moment, before Nisa smiled gently. “Of course, Lex. This actually becomes a good chance for you to see directly the place where everything began.”
That night, the three of them departed together toward the old apartment they had long left, Alex sitting in the car's back seat with great curiosity radiating from his face.
“So this is the place Mama and Father used to live before I was born?” Alex asked throughout the drive.
“Exactly there,” Reza answered from the driver's seat, smiling in remembrance. “The place your Mama first dared to show her DJ talent.”
Returning to where it all began

With help from their old apartment's manager — who still recognized the couple who had once been among the most memorable residents in that complex — Nisa and Reza managed to get access to the unit that had once been their first home, the place where the long journey toward this night first began almost two decades ago.

That room had long been empty, dust covering the floor that had once witnessed their long practices, but its basic structure was still the same — the corner where their mixer table once stood, the window that once always displayed the same Jakarta night view.
“Still the same, isn't it,” Nisa whispered, her eyes gazing far remembering every detail of the first night she seriously learned to DJ in this room, years ago.
Reza smiled, gripping her hand. “Still the same. Only we have changed so much.”

They had brought simple equipment along that night — a portable controller far simpler than the professional equipment they usually used at their music career's peak, but enough for what they planned that night.
One last set

“One last set,” Nisa said, sitting in the chair she'd once sat in awkwardly for the first time years ago, now with the confidence of a woman who had traveled an extraordinarily long journey. “Just for the two of us.”
Reza smiled, sitting beside her. “Just for the two of us.”

Alex, sitting in the room's corner witnessing both his parents with gleaming eyes, smiled understanding that this moment was something very personal for them both. “I'll just watch from here, Ma. This is like watching our family history directly.”
Before they began, Nisa called her son closer. “Come here first, Lex. Try holding this.” She handed the headphones worn out by time into her son's hands. “This is what Mama used when first learning.”
Alex wore those headphones a moment, his eyes widening full of amazement hearing the music flowing. “So cool, Ma. I want to learn someday too.”
“Whenever you're ready, Mama will teach you,” Nisa promised, kissing the top of her son's head before Alex returned to sit in the room's corner, watching with full admiration.

They played for hours that night, not for anyone, not for anything other than themselves — remembering every phase of their journey through songs that had once been the soundtrack of their lives. The first song they played together at the small Kemang cafe years ago. The song accompanying their debut at DWP. Melodies from various regions they'd encountered throughout the Nusantara Bersuara Tour, rearranged with the personal touch that had become their characteristic.
“Do you remember this song?” Nisa asked, playing a familiar track, smiling in remembrance.
“The song we played in Pak Hendra's village,” Reza smiled widely. “I'll never forget that night.”

They kept playing, laughing remembering small mistakes from the past, awkward moments that now felt so sweet to remember, the long journey that had shaped them into the most whole versions of themselves.

Between their playing, memories from that entire long journey flowed heavily in Nisa's mind — the first night she was honest with Reza about her small Numark, their debut at the Kemang cafe full of nervousness, the moment she cried in Reza's embrace after finally opening her deepest wound, Alex's birth that changed everything, the thousands of kilometers they traveled around the country, the storm of attacks that nearly made them waver, to the victory night that still felt like a dream.

“You know,” Nisa said between their playing, her voice trembling with overflowing emotion, “if someone had told me years ago, when I was still secretly listening to EDM in my room, that this journey would bring me to this point… I would never have believed it.”

“But here we are,” Reza gripped her hand a moment, stopping their playing. “Not merely because of luck, Nis. But because of your courage to be your true self, from the first day we started learning together in this room.”
Reflection at night's end

At the end of the night, as the last song began to fade, Reza removed his headphones, looking deep at his wife — the woman he had loved since their first meeting at The Corrs concert years ago, who would now become the leader of the nation they both loved wholeheartedly.
“Ready, Madam President?” he asked gently, his smile full of indescribable pride.
Nisa laughed a little, though her eyes were teary. “Never truly ready, Za. But I believe this is the path I have to take. And I believe, with you beside me, I can face whatever awaits.”
“Always beside you, Nis,” Reza gripped her hand tightly. “From this small studio, to wherever this journey takes us next.”

They sat in comfortable silence for a while, letting the memories from almost two decades of their journey flow in each of their minds — from two young people newly married with dreams and courage, to a couple who had built sturdy foundations in various fields, to tonight, at the threshold of the biggest chapter in their lives.
“Za,” Nisa said finally, her voice full of long-settled emotion, “thank you for always believing in me. Even when I myself doubted.”
“Nothing needs thanking, Nis,” Reza kissed her forehead gently. “This is both our journey. It will always be that way.”
Leaving the studio for the last time

Toward dawn, they finally rose from that small studio, bringing along the simple equipment that had accompanied them that night, leaving the room that had become a silent witness of the beginning of their extraordinary journey.

At the doorway, Nisa stopped a moment, looking back toward the empty room that would now return to silence, perhaps forever, or perhaps awaiting a new occupant who would never know the history that had once happened within it.
“Thank you,” she whispered softly to that room, as if that room were a living entity that had witnessed and supported every step of their journey. “For everything.”
Reza gripped her hand, guiding her out gently. “Time to step into the next chapter, Nis.”

Alex, walking beside them, gripped both his parents' hands. “Ma, Pa,” he said softly, his voice full of earnestness rarely heard from a child his age, “I'm so proud to have seen tonight. I understand now, why Mama is so loved by everyone. Because Mama never forgot where Mama came from.”
Nisa stopped a moment, embracing her son tightly, tears of emotion again pooling in her eyes. “Thank you, Lex. Your words just now, that means more than you know.”

They walked together toward the car that had been waiting, leaving the small studio that had become the starting point of a journey that would soon reach its peak — a journey that began from a simple beat on a rainy night years ago, and would now soon carry them toward Istana Negara, toward a new chapter they had long prepared for with all their heart, love, and sacrifice that was never in vain.

Outside, Jakarta's sky began showing a new orange streak of dawn — a sign of new days that would soon begin, not only for Nisa and Reza, but for the whole nation that had long awaited a leader who truly understood and loved them, from Sabang to Merauke, one beat at a time.
26: October 20, 2044

The inauguration of Nisa Shabrina Farha as the tenth President of the Republic of Indonesia proceeded solemnly at the MPR Building, witnessed by millions of pairs of eyes throughout the country — many of them people who had once known her through bass beats and twinkling stage lights, not through political speeches or conventional campaign billboards.

In the VVIP seats, Reza Satria sat in a neat suit far different from the t-shirt and headphones once identical with him — but his smile, the warmth of his eyes as he watched his wife take the oath of office, had never changed since the first night they sat side by side in front of the mixer table years ago.

Alex, who was now almost fifteen years old, sat beside his father, his back straight full of pride witnessing his mother speak the oath that would change not only their family's life, but also the direction of the nation they had long loved together.
The binding oath

“By Allah, I swear to fulfill the obligations of President of the Republic of Indonesia to the best and most just of my ability, to hold firmly to the Constitution and carry out all its laws and regulations as straightly as possible…”

Nisa's voice echoed in that large room, firm and clear, marking the end of the long chapter of the journey they had traveled together since the first night in their apartment's small studio, almost two decades ago.

When the inauguration procession finished and thunderous applause filled the room, Nisa turned briefly toward her family — Reza looking at her with teary eyes full of pride, Alex smiling widely waving his small hand proudly. A brief but meaningful moment, reminding her that behind the great title she had just officially borne, she remained a wife and mother who loved her family wholeheartedly.
The journey traveled

Amid the thunder of celebration and ceaselessly flowing congratulations, Nisa's mind drifted briefly back to the entire long journey that had brought her to this point — from a young girl hiding her love for EDM behind her hijab, from the threat of forced marriage that nearly seized her entire future, from the first night she dared to be honest with Reza about her small Numark, from the revelation of the deepest wound that changed everything, from Alex's birth that became a new source of strength, from the thousands of kilometers they traveled around the archipelago, listening to millions of voices that all this time were rarely truly heard, from the storm of attacks that nearly made them waver but never truly brought them down.

Every one of those steps, every tear, every small and large victory, now flowed into this moment — not as the end of a journey, but as the beginning of a far bigger chapter, which would test everything she had learned and built throughout the last almost two decades.
“Mother,” Alex whispered, approaching after the procession finished, embracing his mother tightly, “I'm so proud to be Madam President's child.”

Nisa embraced her son tightly, the tears of emotion she'd long held back finally flowing freely. “And Mother is so proud to have a child as strong and mature as you, Lex. This journey, this is your journey too.”
The first days

The first days as head of state brought Nisa directly into a vortex of responsibility far greater than anything she'd ever imagined — marathon meetings with the newly formed cabinet, in-depth briefings about the state's fiscal condition far more complex than it appeared on the surface, meetings with international delegations wanting to immediately establish communication with Indonesia's new leader.

“This is far heavier than I imagined, Za,” Nisa admitted one night, a few days after the inauguration, exhaustion clearly radiating from her face after a marathon meeting until dawn discussing budget deficit projections that urgently needed handling.

Reza, who had now officially taken a new role as the president's spouse while still overseeing Reza Satria Group from a distance, embraced her gently. “You've prepared for almost two decades for this moment, Nis. This exhaustion is natural, but I fully believe, you have everything needed to face this.”
Toward the days to come

Ten days after that inauguration, exactly on October 30 — the day they had celebrated every year as their wedding anniversary since that historic moment at a grand mosque years ago — Nisa and Reza would celebrate nineteen years of their marriage, this time in a way they'd never imagined before: as President of the Republic of Indonesia and her spouse, amid the palace busyness they had just begun to undertake.

However that night, at the end of the first long day as head of state, Nisa stood briefly at the window of their new room at Istana Negara, gazing at Jakarta stretching wide before her — a city that had witnessed every phase of their journey, from a small studio full of dreams, to magnificent stages, to remote villages at the country's ends, to tonight, at the heart of the nation's highest power.
Reza joined beside her, gripping her hand tightly as he always did at every important moment of their journey.
“We made it, Za,” Nisa whispered, her voice trembling with emotion that had long settled throughout this extraordinary journey.
“We made it, Nis,” Reza kissed her forehead gently. “And this is just the beginning of the next chapter.”

In the distance, Jakarta's lights kept twinkling ceaselessly, silent witnesses of an extraordinary journey that had brought two people — who once had only dreams, courage, and love that never dimmed — from a small studio in a simple apartment, to the heart of Istana Negara, carrying along the millions of hopes of the people they had met, listened to, and loved throughout a journey that began from one simple beat, almost two decades ago.

Their journey toward the Palace had only just begun — and the next chapter, full of challenges, big decisions, and struggles that would test everything they had built together, awaited to be traveled, one day, one decision, one beat at a time.
